# 1. Motivation and overview

Classical quantile regression (QR) models the conditional quantiles of a dependent variable as linear functions of predictors, which allows the researcher to study heterogeneous effects across the distribution of the response rather than only at the mean (Koenker and Bassett, 1978; Koenker and Hallock, 2001; Koenker, 2005). In its standard formulation, however, QR treats the regressors as fixed conditioning variables and delivers coefficients that vary with the quantile index of the *response* but not with the quantile index of the *regressor*.

In many empirical applications this is restrictive. The effect of a regressor on the outcome may differ not only across the conditional quantiles of the dependent variable but also across the distribution of the regressor itself. For example, the impact of very large shocks in a financial variable on the upper tail of a risk measure may differ from the impact of more moderate movements around its centre, and those differences may be asymmetric between the lower and upper tails of the outcome distribution.

Quantile-on-quantile regression (QQR), introduced by Sim and Zhou (2015), addresses this limitation by modelling the effect of specific quantiles of a regressor on specific quantiles of a dependent variable. Instead of returning a one-dimensional curve of slopes indexed only by the outcome quantile, QQR yields a two-dimensional surface of slopes indexed jointly by quantiles of the regressor and quantiles of the response. This allows the researcher to investigate, for example, how the effect of extreme realisations of the regressor compares with the effect of more central realisations and how that comparison varies across the outcome distribution. QQR has been used in several recent empirical studies, including applications in energy and environmental economics and finance (e.g. Shahzad et al., 2020).

The `qqrtools` package implements a practical version of QQR based on local linear quantile regression. Conceptually, the package carries out a sequence of weighted QR fits, each centred at a grid point in the support of a designated *quantile regressor*. At each grid point and for each conditional quantile level of the dependent variable, a local linear QR is estimated using kernel weights that emphasise observations whose regressor values lie close to the grid location. The resulting estimates are stored as three dimensional coefficient and p value surfaces for the intercept, the quantile regressor and any additional control variables.

This vignette explains the underlying statistical model, the local estimation strategy, automatic bandwidth selection, and how the exported functions in `qqrtools` map to the mathematical objects defined by the QQR framework. Throughout, the dependent variable is denoted by \(Y\), the designated quantile regressor by \(X\), and additional controls by a vector \(W\).

# Classical quantile regression

##  Conditional quantiles

Let \((Y_t, X_t, W_t)\) for \(t = 1,\ldots,T\) be independent observations from the joint distribution of a scalar dependent variable \(Y\), a scalar regressor \(X\), and a vector of controls \(W\). For a quantile index \(\tau \in (0,1)\), the conditional \(\tau\)-quantile of \(Y\) given \(X = x\) and \(W = w\) is defined as
\[
Q_Y(\tau \mid X = x, W = w)
=
\inf \{ y \in \mathbb{R} : F_{Y \mid X,W}(y \mid x,w) \ge \tau \},
\]
where \(F_{Y \mid X,W}(\cdot \mid x,w)\) is the conditional distribution function of \(Y\) given \((X,W) = (x,w)\) (Koenker and Bassett, 1978).

A linear quantile regression model specifies this conditional quantile as
\[
Q_Y(\tau \mid X = x, W = w)
=
\beta_0(\tau) + \beta_1(\tau)\, x + \gamma(\tau)^{\top} w,
\]
where \(\beta_0(\tau)\) is an intercept, \(\beta_1(\tau)\) is the slope on the regressor \(X\), and \(\gamma(\tau)\) is a vector of slopes on the controls. Collecting the coefficients in the vector
\[
\beta(\tau)
=
\big( \beta_0(\tau), \beta_1(\tau), \gamma(\tau)^{\top} \big)^{\top},
\]
the standard QR estimator \(\hat\beta(\tau)\) solves
\[
\hat\beta(\tau)
=
\arg\min_{\beta}
\sum_{t = 1}^{T}
\rho_{\tau} \big( Y_t - Z_t^{\top} \beta \big),
\]
where \(Z_t = (1, X_t, W_t^{\top})^{\top}\) is the vector of regressors and
\[
\rho_{\tau}(u)
=
u \, \big( \tau - \mathbf{1}\{ u < 0 \} \big)
\]
is the check loss function (Koenker, 2005).

The family of quantile specific slopes \(\{ \beta_1(\tau), \gamma(\tau) : \tau \in (0,1)\}\) describes how the effect of the regressors varies across the distribution of the dependent variable. However, these slopes are functions only of \(\tau\) and do not vary explicitly with the distribution of the regressor \(X\).

## Limitations for distributional heterogeneity in regressors

In many settings the regressor \(X\) itself shows pronounced distributional heterogeneity, and the relationship between \(Y\) and \(X\) may differ markedly between low, middle and high values of \(X\). Standard QR treats such heterogeneity implicitly within a single linear index in \(X\) at each \(\tau\). The resulting coefficient \(\beta_1(\tau)\) can be interpreted as an *average* marginal effect of \(X\) at conditional quantile level \(\tau\), but it is not allowed to vary with the quantile of \(X\).

As a consequence, standard QR can mask interactions between extreme values of \(X\) and extreme values of \(Y\), and it can be difficult to identify non linear or asymmetric patterns that occur only in specific regions of the joint distribution of \((Y,X)\) (Sim and Zhou, 2015; Shahzad et al., 2020). For example, dependence in the lower left tail or upper right tail of the joint distribution may be important in risk management and climate economics, yet it may be attenuated when the model conditions only on the level of \(X\).

Quantile on quantile regression responds to this limitation by constructing a two dimensional mapping
\[
(\tau,\theta) \mapsto \beta_1(\tau,\theta),
\]
where \(\beta_1(\tau,\theta)\) captures how the effect of \(X\) on \(Y\) varies jointly across the \(\tau\)-quantiles of the dependent variable and the \(\theta\)-quantiles of the regressor. This perspective is particularly valuable when interest centres on tail dependence, regime dependent relationships or state dependent transmission mechanisms, which are often smoothed out in models that only index effects by the quantiles of the dependent variable.

#  Quantile-on-quantile regression

##  Conceptual formulation

Let \(Q_X(\theta)\) denote the \(\theta\)-th quantile of the marginal distribution of \(X\), for \(\theta \in (0,1)\). The central object in QQR is the conditional \(\tau\)-quantile of \(Y\) evaluated at a particular quantile of \(X\),
\[
Q_Y\big(\tau \mid X = Q_X(\theta), W = w \big),
\]
which is a function of the two quantile indices \(\tau\) and \(\theta\).

Following Sim and Zhou (2015), this conditional quantile can be approximated by a local linear expansion of the form
\[
Q_Y\big(\tau \mid X \approx Q_X(\theta), W = w \big)
\approx
\alpha(\tau,\theta)
+
\beta(\tau,\theta)\, \big( X - Q_X(\theta) \big)
+
\gamma(\tau,\theta)^{\top} w.
\]
Here

* \(\alpha(\tau,\theta)\) is a local intercept, capturing the conditional \(\tau\)-quantile of \(Y\) when \(X\) is near \(Q_X(\theta)\) and the controls are set to zero;

* \(\beta(\tau,\theta)\) is a local slope on the quantile regressor, describing how small changes in \(X\) in a neighbourhood of \(Q_X(\theta)\) affect the \(\tau\)-th conditional quantile of \(Y\);

* \(\gamma(\tau,\theta)\) is a vector of local slopes on the control variables.

For a given grid of outcome quantiles \(T \subset (0,1)\) and a grid of regressor quantiles \(\Theta \subset (0,1)\), the collection
\[
\big\{ \beta(\tau,\theta) : \tau \in T, \theta \in \Theta \big\}
\]
forms a *slope surface* that describes how the marginal impact of \(X\) varies jointly across the distributions of both \(Y\) and \(X\). When controls are omitted, the model reduces to a bivariate QQR specification. When controls are included, the QQR slope surface for \(X\) is interpreted conditionally on those controls.

##  Local linear quantile regression

The local approximation above is implemented using local linear quantile regression, which generalises local polynomial regression to conditional quantiles (Fan and Gijbels, 1996; Yu and Jones, 1998).

Fix a quantile index \(\theta \in (0,1)\) for the regressor and let \(q_{\theta}\) denote its empirical counterpart, for example the empirical \(\theta\)-quantile of the sample \(\{X_t\}_{t=1}^{T}\). For each observation \(t\), define the localised regressor
\[
Z_t(\theta) = X_t - q_{\theta},
\]
which measures deviations of \(X_t\) from the reference point \(q_{\theta}\).

To emphasise observations for which \(X_t\) lies close to \(q_{\theta}\), introduce kernel weights of the form
\[
w_t(\theta)
=
K\!\left( \frac{X_t - q_{\theta}}{h} \right),
\]
where \(K(\cdot)\) is a kernel function (Gaussian in `qqrtools`) and \(h > 0\) is a bandwidth parameter that controls the degree of smoothing. This is the default, `kernel_space = "x"`, with \(h\) measured in the units of \(X\). In the original formulation of QQR (Sim and Zhou, 2015) the kernel is instead applied to the difference between the empirical distribution function and the quantile index,
\[
w_t(\theta) = K\!\left( \frac{F_n(X_t) - \theta}{h} \right),
\]
so that \(h\) is on the probability scale (Sim and Zhou use \(h = 0.05\)). This weighting is available with `kernel_space = "cdf"`. The two weightings are not identical: in regressor space the effective window contains more observations where the density of \(X\) is high, whereas on the CDF scale every window contains approximately the same share \(\approx h\) of the sample. In both cases the regressor enters the local model as \(X_t - q_\theta\), so \(\hat\beta\) is measured per unit of \(X\).

Conditional on \(\theta\) and \(\tau\), the local linear QQR estimator \((\hat\alpha(\tau,\theta), \hat\beta(\tau,\theta), \hat\gamma(\tau,\theta))\) is obtained by solving the weighted quantile regression problem
\[
(\hat\alpha(\tau,\theta), \hat\beta(\tau,\theta), \hat\gamma(\tau,\theta))
=
\arg\min_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}
\sum_{t=1}^{T}
w_t(\theta)\,
\rho_{\tau}\big( Y_t - \alpha - \beta Z_t(\theta) - \gamma^{\top} W_t \big),
\]
with \(\rho_{\tau}(\cdot)\) defined as in Section 2.1. This optimisation problem has the same structure as a weighted linear QR and can therefore be implemented using existing QR algorithms such as those in the `quantreg` package (Koenker, 2005).

### Local quadratic fitting (`degree = 2`) {-}

The slope \(\beta(\tau,\theta)\) is a first derivative of the conditional quantile function with respect to \(X\). For derivative estimation by local polynomials, the theory of Fan and Gijbels (1996, Chapter 3) shows that a polynomial whose degree exceeds the order of the derivative by an odd number is preferable: for the first derivative, a local *quadratic* rather than a local linear fit. The reason is the behaviour near the boundary of the support of \(X\), which is exactly where the extreme quantiles \(\theta\) of a QQR grid are located. The local linear slope has a bias of order \(h\) there, because the kernel window is cut off on one side and the fit averages the slope over an asymmetric neighbourhood; the local quadratic slope has a bias of order \(h^2\) in the interior and at the boundary. The same results hold for local polynomial quantile regression (Chaudhuri, 1991).

With `degree = 2`, the default, `qqr()` therefore solves
\[
\min_{\alpha,\beta,\delta,\gamma}
\sum_{t=1}^{T} w_t(\theta)\,
\rho_{\tau}\big( Y_t - \alpha - \beta Z_t(\theta) - \delta Z_t(\theta)^2 - \gamma^{\top} W_t \big),
\]
and reports \(\hat\alpha\), \(\hat\beta\) and \(\hat\gamma\); the curvature coefficient \(\hat\delta\) is a nuisance parameter and is not stored. With `degree = 1` the term \(\delta Z_t(\theta)^2\) is omitted, which gives the local linear estimator of Sim and Zhou (2015). The price of the lower bias is a larger variance at a given bandwidth, which is why the local quadratic fit is combined with the wider, slope-oriented default bandwidth described in Section 3.5. The simulation evidence for this combination is summarised there.

Repeating this procedure over a grid of regressor quantiles \(\theta \in \Theta\) and outcome quantiles \(\tau \in T\) yields estimates of

* the local intercept surface \(\hat\alpha(\tau,\theta)\);

* the local slope surface for the quantile regressor \(\hat\beta(\tau,\theta)\);

* the local slope surfaces \(\hat\gamma_k(\tau,\theta)\) for each component \(W_k\) of the control vector.

The local models are indexed by a grid of quantile levels \(\theta_i\) and the corresponding regressor locations \(z_i = q_{\theta_i}\).

##  Discrete grid representation

The continuous surfaces \(\beta(\tau,\theta)\) and \(\gamma_k(\tau,\theta)\) are approximated numerically by evaluating them on finite grids of outcome quantiles and regressor locations. Let
\[
T = \{\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_J\} \subset (0,1)
\]
denote a set of outcome quantile levels and let
\[
G = \{z_1,\ldots,z_M\}
\]
denote a grid of values in the support of \(X\). By default (`grid = "quantile"`) the grid points are the empirical quantiles of the designated quantile regressor,
\[
z_i = \hat Q_X(\theta_i), \qquad
\theta_i = 0.05 + \frac{i-1}{m-1}\,0.90, \quad i = 1,\ldots,m,
\]
or at user-supplied levels `thetas`. With `grid = "range"` the grid consists of \(m\) equally spaced points between the sample minimum and maximum,
\[
z_i
=
\min_{t} X_t
+
\frac{i - 1}{m - 1}
\big( \max_{t} X_t - \min_{t} X_t \big);
\]
the corresponding quantile levels are then \(\theta_i = F_n(z_i)\), which are not equally spaced. The fitted object stores both `grid` (\(z_i\)) and `thetas` (\(\theta_i\)), and the three-dimensional plots use `thetas` on their horizontal axis.

For each grid point \(z_i\) and outcome quantile \(\tau_j\), a local linear QR is fitted using kernel weights
\[
w_t(z_i)
=
K\!\left( \frac{X_t - z_i}{h} \right)
\quad\text{or}\quad
K\!\left( \frac{F_n(X_t) - \theta_i}{h} \right),
\]
which yields estimates \((\hat\alpha_{ij}, \hat\beta_{ij}, \hat\gamma_{ij})\) for the intercept, the quantile regressor and each control variable. The collection of local estimates for the quantile regressor slopes can be organised as an \(m \times J\) matrix
\[
\hat\beta
=
[\hat\beta_{ij}]_{i=1,\ldots,m}^{\quad j=1,\ldots,J},
\]
and similarly for the intercept and control coefficient surfaces:
\[
\hat\alpha
=
[\hat\alpha_{ij}]_{i=1,\ldots,m}^{\quad j=1,\ldots,J},
\quad
\hat\gamma_k
=
[\hat\gamma_{k,ij}]_{i=1,\ldots,m}^{\quad j=1,\ldots,J}
\quad
\text{for each control } k.
\]

From a computational perspective, a fitted QQR model can therefore be represented by

* the grid vector \(G = (z_1,\ldots,z_m)\);

* the quantile vector \(T = (\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_J)\); and

* a list of coefficient matrices \(\{\hat\alpha, \hat\beta, \hat\gamma_1,\ldots,\hat\gamma_K\}\).

This is precisely the structure stored internally by the `qqrtools` package and exposed to users through its various methods and helper functions.

## Local sample information and standard errors

The reliability of the local estimates \(\hat\beta_{ij}\) depends on the effective amount of information available near each grid point. Given the kernel weights \(\{w_t(z_i)\}_{t=1}^{T}\), `qqrtools` reports the Kish effective sample size
\[
n_{\text{eff}}(z_i)
=
\frac{\big(\sum_{t=1}^{T} w_t(z_i)\big)^2}{\sum_{t=1}^{T} w_t(z_i)^2}
\]
in `effective_n`. It does not depend on \(\tau_j\) but is stored as an \(m \times J\) matrix aligned with the surfaces. Local fits with \(n_{\text{eff}}\) smaller than the number of coefficients plus one, a rank-deficient weighted design, or a solver error are not estimated: the cells are `NA`, they are counted in `n_failed`, and `qqr()` issues one warning.

For inference, standard errors and p values for the coefficients at each \((z_i,\tau_j)\) are obtained by applying standard QR variance estimators to the local weighted QR models. The `qqrtools` package delegates this task to the `summary.rq` function from `quantreg`, which offers several options for the estimation of standard errors, including independent normal approximations, kernel based estimators, and bootstrap methods (Koenker and Hallock, 2001; Koenker, 2005). The user chooses the type of standard errors through the `se_type` argument, and the resulting p values are stored in matrices that are aligned with the corresponding coefficient surfaces.

These p values treat each weighted local problem as if it were a parametric linear QR model. They are **pointwise** and do not account for the smoothing bias of the local linear approximation, the data-dependent choice of \(h\), or the fact that \(m \times J\) cells are examined at once. They are best read as descriptive indicators of where the surface is clearly different from zero, not as formal tests with exact size; the simulation evidence in `audit/ECONOMETRIC_VALIDATION_REPORT.md` quantifies their behaviour in simple designs.

### Choice of standard errors {-}

The behaviour of the three standard-error types was examined in designs without any effect (\(Y\) independent of \(X\); normal and skewed \(X\); \(n = 250\) and \(1000\); default bandwidth and degree; 300 replications; script `tools/validation/size_default.R`). A test at the 5% level should then reject in 5% of the cells.

| design | n | se_type | pooled_rejection_rate | max_cell_rate | any_cell_significant | any_cell_significant_BH |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| N | 250 | nid | 0.093 | 0.170 | 0.820 | 0.407 |
| N | 250 | ker | 0.035 | 0.090 | 0.483 | 0.060 |
| N | 250 | boot | 0.050 | 0.077 | 0.577 | 0.087 |
| N | 1000 | nid | 0.079 | 0.153 | 0.747 | 0.280 |
| N | 1000 | ker | 0.042 | 0.080 | 0.513 | 0.080 |
| N | 1000 | boot | 0.050 | 0.080 | 0.567 | 0.087 |
| S | 250 | nid | 0.076 | 0.157 | 0.740 | 0.263 |
| S | 250 | ker | 0.042 | 0.093 | 0.517 | 0.083 |
| S | 250 | boot | 0.050 | 0.067 | 0.500 | 0.097 |
| S | 1000 | nid | 0.074 | 0.150 | 0.767 | 0.237 |
| S | 1000 | ker | 0.044 | 0.100 | 0.563 | 0.097 |
| S | 1000 | boot | 0.052 | 0.073 | 0.613 | 0.103 |

Tests based on `"nid"` reject too often (7--9% on average and up to 17% in single cells), tests based on `"ker"`, the Powell kernel sandwich, are slightly conservative (3.5--4.4%), and bootstrap tests are close to the nominal level. The default is therefore `se_type = "ker"`, which is fast and deterministic; `se_type = "boot"` (after `set.seed()`) is recommended for results that are reported, at a higher computational cost. The last two columns show why the adjustment for multiplicity described next matters: without it, about half of all surfaces contain at least one "significant" cell although there is no effect anywhere.

### Multiplicity (`qqr_padjust()`) {-}

A surface with the default settings has \(19 \times 19 = 361\) cells per coefficient, so about 18 cells are expected to have \(p < 0.05\) when there is no effect anywhere. `qqr_padjust()` replaces each p-value surface by p-values adjusted over all cells of that surface with `stats::p.adjust()`. The default controls the false discovery rate with the procedure of Benjamini and Hochberg (1995), which remains valid under the positive dependence that is typical for neighbouring cells; `method = "BY"` (Benjamini and Yekutieli, 2001) is valid under arbitrary dependence and more conservative; `"holm"` and `"bonferroni"` control the family-wise error rate. All tables, exports and significance overlays use the adjusted values of the returned object.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
fit_adj <- qqr_padjust(fit)            # Benjamini-Hochberg
fit_by  <- qqr_padjust(fit, "BY")      # Benjamini-Yekutieli
```

The adjustment addresses multiplicity only. Smoothing bias and bandwidth selection are still ignored, and uniform confidence bands for conditional quantile processes (Qu and Yoon, 2015) are not implemented.

## Bandwidth selection

### Why automatic selection matters {-}

The bandwidth \(h\) is the single most influential tuning parameter in QQR. Too small a bandwidth yields a noisy, erratic surface because each local regression is based on very few effectively weighted observations; too large a bandwidth smooths over genuine local heterogeneity in the coefficient surface. Because a researcher can, intentionally or not, choose \(h\) post hoc to produce a surface that appears more interesting or confirms a prior hypothesis, free bandwidth selection constitutes a form of specification searching that undermines the credibility of the findings.

The `qqrtools` package addresses this by making **automatic bandwidth selection the default**. Ten data-driven selectors are provided via the `h` argument of `qqr()`. In every case the selected bandwidth, the formula used to compute it, and the numerical inputs are stored in the fitted object under `h_method` and `h_details` and are printed by `print.qqr()` and `summary.qqr()`, so the selection can be reported transparently in a paper's methods section.

### Slope-oriented rule of thumb (`h = "slope"`, default) {-}

$$
h_{\text{slope}} = C\,\min\!\left(\hat\sigma_X,\;\frac{\widehat{\mathrm{IQR}}_X}{1.34}\right) n^{-1/7},
\qquad C = 2 .
$$
The classical rules of thumb below are of order \(n^{-1/5}\), the optimal rate for estimating a density or the *level* of a regression function. The object of interest in QQR is a *slope*. The variance of a local polynomial estimate of a first derivative is of order \(1/(n h^{3})\) instead of \(1/(n h)\), and with a squared bias of order \(h^{4}\) the mean squared error is minimised by a bandwidth of order \(n^{-1/7}\) (Fan and Gijbels, 1996, Chapter 3). A bandwidth chosen for the level is therefore systematically too small for the slope, and the difference grows with the sample size. The rule uses the robust scale estimate of Silverman (1986) so that heavy tails do not inflate the bandwidth.

The rate is given by theory, but the optimal constant depends on unknown features of the data (the third derivative of the conditional quantile function and the conditional density of the errors). The constant \(C = 2\) was therefore calibrated by simulation in three designs with uniform, normal and skewed regressors and linear, sinusoidal and saturating slopes (script `tools/validation/bandwidth_calibration.R` in the source repository). The table reports the root mean squared error of the slope, averaged over a \(5 \times 5\) grid of \((\theta,\tau)\) cells, relative to the best rule in each row.

| Design, n | C = 2, quadratic (default) | C = 1.5, quadratic | C = 2.5, quadratic | C = 2, linear | Silverman, linear |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| D1 (uniform X), n = 250 | 1.29 | 1.58 | 1.15 | 1.01 | 1.86 |
| D1 (uniform X), n = 1000 | 1.28 | 1.61 | 1.10 | 1.28 | 2.30 |
| D2 (normal X), n = 250 | 1.12 | 1.00 | 1.27 | 1.81 | 1.21 |
| D2 (normal X), n = 1000 | 1.28 | 1.07 | 1.54 | 2.51 | 1.25 |
| D3 (skewed X), n = 250 | 1.17 | 1.40 | 1.07 | 1.18 | 1.67 |
| D3 (skewed X), n = 1000 | 1.18 | 1.46 | 1.05 | 1.61 | 2.12 |
| **Worst case** | 1.29 | 1.61 | 1.54 | 2.51 | 2.30 |

Values are RMSE ratios: 1.00 is the best of all 12 rule-degree combinations in that row (constants 1.06, 1.5, 2, 2.5 and 3 with both degrees, and Silverman's rule with both degrees). The default is never more than 29% above the best combination, whereas Silverman's rule with a local linear fit is up to 130% above it. At the same bandwidth (C = 2) the local quadratic fit reduces the mean absolute bias from 0.57 to 0.07 in design D1 and from 0.58 to 0.29 in design D2 at n = 250, at the cost of a larger standard deviation. In the same study `"cv_slope"` improved on `"cv_fast"` in every design but was less accurate than `"slope"`; it is offered for users who prefer a data-driven constant.

With `kernel_space = "cdf"`, the rule is applied to the ranks \(F_n(X_t)\). The rule is a transparent default, not an optimal bandwidth for every data set; Section 3.5 ends with the recommended sensitivity analysis.

### Silverman's rule of thumb (`h = "silverman"`) {-}

$$
h_{\text{Silverman}} = 1.06\,\hat\sigma_X\, n^{-1/5},
$$
where \(\hat\sigma_X\) is the sample standard deviation of the quantile regressor and \(n\) is the sample size (Silverman, 1986). This is the normal-reference bandwidth that minimises the asymptotic mean integrated squared error of a Gaussian-kernel density estimate when the true density is Gaussian. It is fast to compute, requires only the sample standard deviation, and is easy to reproduce and report. It was designed for density estimation and under-smooths QQR slopes.

**Caveat for the density and level rules.** The remaining rules in this section are optimal (under their own assumptions) for estimating a *density* or a *conditional mean*, not for the local *slope* of a conditional quantile. The variance of a local linear slope estimate grows like \(1/(n h^3)\), so bandwidths of order \(n^{-1/5}\) can give noisy slope surfaces in moderate samples; the simulation study in `audit/ECONOMETRIC_VALIDATION_REPORT.md` illustrates this. The automatic rules make the choice transparent and reproducible, but they are not a substitute for reporting \(h\) and checking the sensitivity of the conclusions to larger and smaller bandwidths. With `kernel_space = "cdf"`, the rules are applied to the ranks \(F_n(X_t)\).

### Robust rule of thumb (`h = "robust"`) {-}

$$
h_{\text{robust}}
= 0.9\,\min\!\left(\hat\sigma_X,\;\frac{\widehat{\mathrm{IQR}}_X}{1.34}\right)
n^{-1/5},
$$
where \(\widehat{\mathrm{IQR}}_X\) is the sample interquartile range of the quantile regressor (Silverman, 1986; Scott, 1992). Dividing the IQR by 1.34 converts it to the scale of a standard deviation under normality. The \(\min(\cdot)\) operation selects the smaller of the two scale estimates, which suppresses the influence of heavy tails or outliers. This rule is preferred when the quantile regressor exhibits skewness, leptokurtosis, or outliers -- conditions that are common in financial returns, exchange rates, commodity prices, and other macroeconomic series.

### IQR-based rule (`h = "iqr"`) {-}

$$
h_{\text{IQR}} = \widehat{\mathrm{IQR}}_X\, n^{-1/5}.
$$
This rule scales the bandwidth directly to the interquartile range of the quantile regressor without the standard deviation correction. It is appropriate when the spread of the quantile regressor is better characterised by its interquartile range than by its standard deviation, for example when the variable has a bounded or strongly asymmetric distribution.

### Leave-one-out cross-validation (`h = "cv_fast"`) {-}

The cross-validation selector minimises the out-of-sample check loss of a kernel conditional median of the outcome. Let \(\hat Q_{-t}(0.5 \mid X_t;\,h)\) denote the leave-one-out weighted median of \(\{Y_s\}_{s \neq t}\) with weights \(K((X_s - X_t)/h)\). The CV bandwidth is
$$
h_{\text{CV}}
= \arg\min_{h \in \mathcal{H}}
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}
\rho_{0.5}\!\left(Y_t - \hat Q_{-t}(0.5 \mid X_t;\, h)\right),
$$
where \(\mathcal{H}\) is a 15-point search grid spanning
\([0.5\,h_{\text{Silverman}},\; 2\,h_{\text{Silverman}}]\). Check-loss cross-validation for kernel quantile regression follows Yu and Jones (1998). The criterion is computed at \(\tau = 0.5\) for a local-constant predictor, so it is a pragmatic, data-driven choice rather than an optimal bandwidth for every \(\tau\) or for the local slope; its cost grows with \(n^2\).

### Cross-validation at the slope rate (`h = "cv_slope"`) {-}

$$
h_{\text{CV-slope}} = h_{\text{CV}}\; n^{1/5 - 1/7}.
$$
Cross-validation of the check loss targets the level of the conditional quantile, for which the optimal bandwidth is of order \(n^{-1/5}\). Multiplying by \(n^{1/5-1/7} = n^{2/35}\) moves the data-driven bandwidth to the \(n^{-1/7}\) rate of slope estimation (the factor is 1.37 for \(n = 250\) and 1.48 for \(n = 1000\)). This is a rate adjustment in the spirit of the relation between the optimal bandwidths for a function and its derivatives in Fan and Gijbels (1996); it is data-driven in the constant but, like `"cv_fast"`, costs \(O(n^2)\) operations.

### Sheather-Jones solve-the-equation plug-in (`h = "sj"`) {-}

The Sheather-Jones selector uses base R `bw.SJ(x)` to find the bandwidth
by solving the equation
$$
h = \left[\frac{R(K)}{n\,\hat\psi_4\!\left(g(h)\right)}\right]^{1/5}
$$
iteratively, where \(R(K) = \int K^2(u)\,du\) is the roughness of the
kernel, \(\hat\psi_4 = \int [\hat f''(x)]^2\,dx\) is a pilot estimate
of the integrated squared second derivative of the density, and \(g(h)\) is
a pilot bandwidth for that estimate (Sheather and Jones, 1991). Unlike the
Silverman rule, the SJ plug-in does not assume a particular functional form
for \(f\). It is widely regarded as the best density-based selector
available in base R (Jones, Marron and Sheather, 1996). No additional
packages are required; the selector falls back to the Silverman rule with a
warning if the solve-the-equation iteration fails to converge.

A note on scope: like the Silverman and robust rules, `"sj"` is a
**density-based** selector -- it treats \(X\) alone and does not use the
outcome \(Y\). It therefore selects the bandwidth that is optimal for
estimating the marginal density of the quantile regressor, not for the
conditional quantile surface itself.

###  Ruppert-Sheather-Wand direct plug-in (`h = "yj"`) {-}

The Ruppert-Sheather-Wand (1995) selector uses `KernSmooth::dpill(x, y)` to
minimise the MISE of a local linear regression of the outcome \(Y\) on the
quantile regressor \(X\):
$$
h_{\text{YJ}}
= \left[
    \frac{\hat\sigma^2_\varepsilon\,\int K^2(u)\,du}
         {n\,\hat f_X(x)\,[\hat m''(x)]^2\,\mu_2(K)^2}
  \right]^{1/5},
$$
where \(\hat m''(x)\) is an estimate of the second derivative of the
regression function \(m(x) = E(Y \mid X = x)\), obtained from pilot fits
using Mallows \(C_p\) block sizes (Ruppert, Sheather and Wand, 1995).

This is the **only selector in the suite that uses both \(X\) and \(Y\)**
and that is tuned to regression rather than density loss. It is therefore the
most structurally appropriate automatic selector for QQR, which is
fundamentally a local regression problem (Yu and Jones, 1998). Requires the
`KernSmooth` package, a recommended package that ships with standard R
installations.

###  np full least-squares cross-validation (`h = "npcv"`) and smooth-coefficient cross-validation (`h = "sc"`) {-}

Both selectors use functions from the `np` package (Hayfield and Racine, 2008)
and require `np` to be installed (listed in `Suggests`).

**`"npcv"`** uses `np::npregbw(xdat = x, ydat = y, regtype = "ll")` to
minimise the LOO least-squares loss:
$$
h_{\text{NPCV}}
= \arg\min_{h}
  \frac{1}{n}\sum_{t=1}^{n}
  \left[Y_t - \hat m_{-t}(X_t;\,h)\right]^2,
$$
where \(\hat m_{-t}(X_t;\,h)\) is the leave-one-out local-linear fit at
observation \(t\) using bandwidth \(h\). The `np` implementation uses
generalised product kernels that support mixed continuous and categorical data
(Li and Racine, 2004), making it the most general of all the selectors. It is
also the most computationally intensive.

**`"sc"`** uses `np::npscoefbw(xdat = x, ydat = y)` to select the bandwidth
for the smooth varying-coefficient model
$$
Y_i = W_i^\top \gamma(Z_i) + u_i,
$$
where \(\gamma(Z_i)\) varies smoothly with the conditioning variable
\(Z_i\). This is the closest structural analogue to QQR in least-squares
form: QQR estimates \(\beta(\tau, z_i)\) -- a coefficient vector that
varies with \(z_i\) -- which has exactly the same structure as the
varying-coefficient model, but within a quantile rather than mean regression
framework (Li, Huang, Li and Fu, 2002; Li and Racine, 2010).

###  Manual bandwidth {-}

A positive numeric value may still be passed directly to `h`. This is accepted -- for example to replicate a specific published result -- but triggers a **reproducibility warning** encouraging the researcher to use an automatic method. The warning message reads:

> *"Bandwidth h was set manually to [value]. Manual bandwidth choices affect the results; report them and check sensitivity. Automatic rules: slope, cv_slope, silverman, robust, iqr, cv_fast, sj, yj, npcv, sc."*

The fitted object records `h_method = "manual"` and the `print()` and `summary()` output include a prominent reminder. The following table summarises the recommended choice of method:

| Situation | Recommended method |
|---|---|
| General use | `"slope"` (default) |
| Data-driven constant at the slope rate | `"cv_slope"` |
| Replicating density-rule results | `"silverman"` |
| Distribution better described by quartiles | `"iqr"` |
| No distributional assumptions, no extra packages | `"cv_fast"` |
| Best density-based selector, base R only | `"sj"` |
| Regression data, best structural match to QQR | `"yj"` |
| Mixed-type data, maximum data-driven rigour | `"npcv"` |
| Varying-coefficient structural analogue | `"sc"` |
| Replicating a specific prior result | Numeric `h` with explicit documentation |

### Bandwidth sensitivity analysis (`qqr_sensitivity()`) {-}

No automatic rule removes the dependence of a nonparametric estimate on its bandwidth, and choosing \(h\) after inspecting the results invalidates naive inference. The recommended practice is to fix the rule in advance, report \(h\), and show that the conclusions are stable over a pre-specified range of bandwidths. `qqr_sensitivity()` refits the model for multiples of the selected bandwidth (by default 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.5 and 2) with all other settings unchanged and reports, for each bandwidth, the mean and dispersion of the surface, its correlation with the baseline surface, the share of cells with the same sign, and the mean absolute difference; its `plot()` method shows the grid-averaged slope against \(\tau\) for every bandwidth.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
sens <- qqr_sensitivity(fit)
sens
plot(sens)
```

Features that appear only for the smallest bandwidths are likely to be noise; features that disappear only for the largest bandwidths may be genuine local structure that is being smoothed away.

## Practical considerations

The choice of bandwidth \(h\), the number of grid points \(m\), and the set of quantile levels \(T\) involves trade offs between local detail, smoothness and computation time, similar to other local polynomial procedures (Fan and Gijbels, 1996). Very small bandwidths and very dense grids can reveal fine local structure but may lead to noisy estimates in regions where data are sparse. Larger bandwidths and coarser grids produce smoother surfaces but may blur local features.

Users are encouraged to complement visual inspection of the estimated surfaces with diagnostics based on the effective local sample size and p value surfaces, and where necessary to experiment with different bandwidths and grid sizes. The methods described in this vignette apply for any such choices; `qqrtools` simply implements them in a way that is computationally convenient and aligned with standard QR routines.

# 4. The QQR estimator and its R implementation

## The `qqr()` function and the QQR object

The main user interface in the package is the function
```{r, eval = FALSE}
qqr(
  formula,
  data,
  qvar      = NULL,
  taus      = seq(0.05, 0.95, by = 0.05),
  m         = 19,
  h            = "slope",
  kernel       = c("gaussian"),
  se_type      = c("ker", "nid", "boot", "none"),
  ...,
  na.action    = stats::na.omit,
  grid         = c("quantile", "range"),
  thetas       = NULL,
  kernel_space = c("x", "cdf"),
  degree       = 2
)
```

###  Model specification

The `formula` argument specifies the conditional quantile model for \(Y\) as a linear function of the quantile regressor \(X\) and optional control variables \(W\). For example,

\[
Y = X + z_1 + z_2,
\]

defines \(Y\) as the left hand side, \(X\) as one of the right hand side regressors, and \(W = (Z_1, Z_2)^{\top}\) as additional controls. The `qvar` argument identifies which regressor is to be treated as the quantile regressor whose distribution will be probed by the QQR procedure. In this example, setting `qvar = "X"` designates \(X\) as the quantile regressor and treats \(z_1\) and \(z_2\) as controls.

Internally, `qqr()` constructs a model frame, identifies the dependent and independent variables, and checks that the dependent variable and the quantile regressor are numeric. If multiple regressors are present on the right hand side of the formula, `qvar` must explicitly identify which one plays the role of \(X\). This design matches the conceptual framework in Section 3, in which a specific regressor is singled out as the variable whose distribution is explored through QQR.

### 4.1.2 Grid, bandwidth and kernel

The argument `m` determines the number of grid points in
\[
G = \{z_1,\ldots,z_m\},
\]
constructed at the empirical quantiles of the quantile regressor (`grid = "quantile"`, default; levels `thetas`) or as an equally spaced sequence between its sample minimum and maximum (`grid = "range"`), as in Section 3.3.

The argument `h` controls the bandwidth of the kernel. As detailed in Section 3.5, it accepts either a character string naming an automatic selection method or a positive numeric value. The default is `h = "slope"`. The automatic methods are:

* `"slope"`: \(h = 2\,\min(\hat\sigma_X,\, \widehat{\text{IQR}}_X/1.34)\, n^{-1/7}\). The default. Uses the \(n^{-1/7}\) rate that is optimal for local slopes (Fan and Gijbels, 1996).
* `"cv_slope"`: the `"cv_fast"` bandwidth multiplied by \(n^{1/5-1/7}\).
* `"silverman"`: \(h = 1.06\,\hat\sigma_X\, n^{-1/5}\). Fast, requires only the sample standard deviation. Optimal under normality (Silverman, 1986).
* `"robust"`: \(h = 0.9\,\min(\hat\sigma_X,\, \widehat{\text{IQR}}_X/1.34)\, n^{-1/5}\). Preferred for heavy-tailed or skewed regressors (Silverman, 1986; Scott, 1992).
* `"iqr"`: \(h = \widehat{\text{IQR}}_X\, n^{-1/5}\). Appropriate when spread is best captured by the interquartile range.
* `"cv_fast"`: fast leave-one-out cross-validation over a 15-point grid spanning \([0.5\,h_{\text{Silverman}},\, 2\,h_{\text{Silverman}}]\). Minimises the LOO quantile check-loss at \(\tau = 0.5\). No additional packages required (Yu and Jones, 1998).
* `"sj"`: Sheather-Jones solve-the-equation plug-in. Uses base R `bw.SJ(x)`. Widely regarded as the best density-based selector in base R (Sheather and Jones, 1991).
* `"yj"`: Ruppert-Sheather-Wand direct plug-in. Uses `KernSmooth::dpill(x, y)`. The only selector that uses both \(X\) and \(Y\) and minimises regression MISE, making it the most structurally appropriate for QQR (Ruppert, Sheather and Wand, 1995).
* `"npcv"`: np full least-squares cross-validation via `np::npregbw()`. Minimises LOO squared-error loss; supports mixed data types. Requires the `np` package (Hayfield and Racine, 2008).
* `"sc"`: np smooth-coefficient cross-validation via `np::npscoefbw()`. Selects bandwidth for the varying-coefficient model \(Y_i = W_i^\top \gamma(Z_i) + u_i\) -- the closest structural analogue to QQR in least-squares form. Requires the `np` package (Li and Racine, 2010).

A positive numeric value is also accepted but triggers a reproducibility warning (see Section 3.5.9). The selected or supplied bandwidth, its method label, and a full description are stored in `fit$bandwidth`, `fit$h_method`, and `fit$h_details` respectively, and are printed by `print.qqr()` and `summary.qqr()`.

The default kernel is Gaussian. In mathematical notation it is given by
\[
K(u)
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\!\left( -\frac{u^2}{2} \right),
\]
so that the local weights at grid point \(z_i\) are
\[
w_t(z_i)
=
K\!\left( \frac{X_t - z_i}{h} \right).
\]
These weights enter the objective function for the local linear QR at each grid point as described in Section 3.2. The combination of `m` and `h` governs the balance between local resolution and smoothness of the estimated coefficient surfaces.

### 4.1.3 Coefficient and p value surfaces

For each grid point \(z_i\) and quantile level \(\tau_j\), `qqr()` solves the corresponding weighted QR problem and records:

* \(\hat\alpha_{ij}\): the local intercept;

* \(\hat\beta_{ij}\): the local slope on the quantile regressor;

* \(\hat\gamma_{k,ij}\): the local slopes on each control variable \(W_k\);

* p values for each coefficient, when `se_type` is not `"none"`.

These quantities are stored in two parallel lists of matrices:

* `coef_surfaces`: a named list of coefficient matrices, one for each coefficient in the model;

* `pval_surfaces`: a named list of p value matrices with the same dimensions and names.

If the formula includes an intercept, its internal coefficient name is `"(Intercept)"`. The quantile regressor slope is stored under the actual variable name supplied in `qvar`, and each control variable appears under its own name. The fitted model uses the localised pseudo-regressor
\[
Z_t(z_i) = X_t - z_i
\]
internally for estimation, but the resulting coefficient is stored and accessed through the original variable name. For convenience, the matrix for the quantile regressor slope is also extracted as `qcoef`, so that
\[
\texttt{fit\$qcoef}
=
[\hat\beta_{ij}]_{i=1,\ldots,m}^{\quad j=1,\ldots,J}.
\]

Additional slots in the returned object include:

* `grid`: the numeric vector \((z_1,\ldots,z_m)\);

* `taus`: the vector of outcome quantile levels \((\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_J)\);

* `effective_n`: a matrix of effective local sample sizes \(n_{\text{eff}}(z_i)\);

* `controls`: the names of the control variables \(W\);

* `intercept`: a logical flag indicating whether an intercept was included;

* `bandwidth`, `h_method`, and `h_details`: the numeric bandwidth, the selection method label (e.g. `"silverman"`), and a full description of how \(h\) was chosen, suitable for inclusion in a paper's methods section;

* `n`: the number of observations used in the fit.

The object returned by `qqr()` therefore contains a complete discrete representation of the QQR coefficient surfaces for all coefficients in the model, along with information about the local sample sizes and tuning parameters.

## Printing and summarising QQR objects

### `print.qqr()`

The `print.qqr()` method provides a compact textual description of a fitted QQR model. It reports the original call, the names of the dependent variable, the quantile regressor and any controls, whether an intercept was included, the sample size, the number of grid points and quantiles, the kernel, the SE type, and the bandwidth with its selection method. When `h` was supplied manually, a prominent warning line is included. This output is intended as a diagnostic view of the model specification rather than as a full statistical summary.

### `summary.qqr()` and `print.summary.qqr()`

The `summary.qqr()` method focuses on the slope surface for the quantile regressor,
\[
\hat\beta = [\hat\beta_{ij}]_{i=1,\ldots,m}^{\quad j=1,\ldots,J},
\]
and computes a set of global summaries:

* the range of the grid, \(\min_i z_i\) and \(\max_i z_i\);

* the minimum and maximum values of the slope surface, \(\min_{i,j} \hat\beta_{ij}\) and \(\max_{i,j} \hat\beta_{ij}\);

* the overall mean and standard deviation of the slope values, viewed as the \(m \times J\) collection \(\{\hat\beta_{ij}\}\);

* the row means
\[
\bar\beta_i
=
\frac{1}{J} \sum_{j=1}^{J} \hat\beta_{ij},
\quad
i = 1,\ldots,m,
\]
which average the slope across the outcome quantiles at each grid point;

* the column means
\[
\tilde\beta_j
=
\frac{1}{m} \sum_{i=1}^{m} \hat\beta_{ij},
\quad
j = 1,\ldots,J,
\]
which average the slope across the grid at each outcome quantile.

The associated `print.summary.qqr()` method formats and prints these quantities. The row means \(\{\bar\beta_i\}\) summarise how the average effect of \(X\) varies across its support, while the column means \(\{\tilde\beta_j\}\) summarise how the average effect varies across the quantiles of \(Y\).

The updated `summary.qqr()` object also carries a **bandwidth diagnostics block**, comprising `bandwidth`, `h_method`, `h_details`, `kernel`, `se_type`, and `n`. The `print.summary.qqr()` method formats these into a dedicated section that reports the selection formula, the numerical inputs (\(\hat\sigma_X\), \(\widehat{\text{IQR}}_X\), \(n\)) and the resulting \(h\). This block is designed to be transcribed verbatim into the methods section of a research paper.

## Extracting coefficient surfaces as tables

###  `qqr_surface()`: coefficient and p value tables

The helper function
```{r, eval = FALSE}
qqr_surface(
  x,
  coef               = "all",
  what               = c("coef", "pvalue"),
  grid_subset        = NULL,
  tau_subset         = NULL,
  include_grid_value = TRUE,
  digits             = NULL,
  long               = NULL
)
```
extracts one or more surfaces from a fitted QQR object and returns them in data frame form. Its role is to provide a bridge between the internal matrices and downstream workflows such as plotting, reporting or further analysis.

The argument `what` selects between coefficient matrices \([\hat\alpha_{ij}], [\hat\beta_{ij}], [\hat\gamma_{k,ij}]\) and the corresponding p value matrices. The argument `coef` identifies which coefficients to extract. For example:

* `coef = "X"` returns the surface for the quantile regressor slope, \([\hat\beta_{ij}]\);

* `coef = "intercept"` returns the surface for the intercept, \([\hat\alpha_{ij}]\);

* `coef = "all"` returns all coefficient surfaces.

For a single coefficient and `long = FALSE`, `qqr_surface()` returns a wide matrix like data frame with rows indexed by grid points and columns indexed by quantile levels. The typical structure is
\[
\text{Grid}_{\text{Point}},\quad 
\text{Grid}_{\text{Value}},\quad
\tau_{\tau_1}, \ldots, \tau_{\tau_J}
\]

This representation corresponds directly to the matrix \([\hat\beta_{ij}]\) in Section 3.3, with `Grid_Point` indicating the index \(i\), `Grid_Value` giving \(z_i\), and the `tau_*` columns providing \(\hat\beta_{ij}\) for each \(j\).

When multiple coefficients are requested or `long = TRUE`, `qqr_surface()` returns a tidy long data frame with one row per coefficient--grid--quantile triple:
\[
(\text{Coefficient},\ \text{Grid}_{\text{Point}},\ \text{Grid}_{\text{Value}},\ \tau,\ \hat{\beta}_{ij})
\]

which is convenient for tidy workflows and flexible plotting systems. The `digits` argument allows the user to apply rounding for presentation without affecting the underlying QQR object.

### `rowave.qqr()`: row wise averages across quantiles

The function
```{r, eval = FALSE}
rowave.qqr(
  x,
  coef   = "all",
  na.rm  = TRUE,
  digits = NULL,
  ...
)
```
computes row means of the coefficient surfaces across all outcome quantiles. When `coef = "all"`, it constructs, for each coefficient \(k\), the summary
\[
\bar\beta_{k,i}
=
\frac{1}{J} \sum_{j=1}^{J} \hat\beta_{k,ij},
\quad
i = 1,\ldots,m,
\]
and returns a data frame with columns
\[
\text{grid}_{\text{index}},\quad
\text{grid}_{\text{value}},\quad
\bar{\beta}_{\text{Intercept},\,i},\quad
\bar{\beta}_{X,i},\quad
\bar{\beta}_{W_1,i},\ldots
\]

For a single coefficient, for example `coef = "X"`, the function returns a data frame with `grid_index`, `grid_value` and one column, say `mean_X`, containing the row means \(\bar\beta_i\) as defined in Section 4.2.2. This provides a compact one dimensional summary of how the average slope for a given coefficient varies across the support of the quantile regressor.

Again, the `digits` argument only affects the formatting of the returned data frame and not the stored QQR object.

## Visualising QQR surfaces

### `plot.qqr()`: static three dimensional surfaces

The S3 method
```{r, eval = FALSE}
plot(
  x,
  coef   = x$independent,
  what   = c("coef", "pvalue"),
  engine = c("plot3D", "base"),
  ...
)
```
produces a three dimensional perspective plot of a selected surface from a QQR object. Internally, it retrieves the matrix \([\hat\beta_{ij}]\) or \([\hat p_{ij}]\), where \(\hat p_{ij}\) is the p value associated with the coefficient at \((z_i,\tau_j)\), and uses either base graphics or the `plot3D` package to plot the surface against the grid and quantile axes.

Mathematically, the plot shows the function
\[
(z_i,\tau_j) \mapsto \hat\beta_{ij}
\quad \text{or} \quad
(z_i,\tau_j) \mapsto \hat p_{ij},
\]
with the horizontal axes corresponding to the regressor grid and the outcome quantiles \(\tau_j\), and the vertical axis showing either coefficient values or p values.

By visualising \(\hat\beta_{ij}\) as a surface, the user can directly inspect patterns such as:

* changes in the sign or magnitude of the slope across regions of the regressor distribution;

* clustering of significant effects in particular areas of the joint quantile space;

* non linearities or asymmetries that would be difficult to detect from one dimensional summaries alone.

### `Int.plot()`: interactive three dimensional surfaces

The generic function
```{r, eval = FALSE}
Int.plot(x, ...)
```
with method
```{r, eval = FALSE}
Int.plot.qqr(
  x,
  coef      = x$independent,
  what      = c("coef", "pvalue"),
  add_plane = FALSE,
  plane_z   = 0,
  ...
)
```
uses the `rgl` package to produce interactive three dimensional visualisations of the same surfaces. The method maps each grid--quantile pair \((z_i,\tau_j)\) to a point in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) with coordinates \((z_i,\tau_j,\hat\beta_{ij})\) or \((z_i,\tau_j,\hat p_{ij})\) and renders them in an interactive window where users can rotate, zoom and change the viewing angle.

An optional reference plane at height `plane_z` can be added to mark, for example, the zero line for coefficients or a chosen significance threshold for p values. In mathematical terms this is the set
\[
\{(x,y,z) \in \mathbb{R}^3 : z = \text{plane}_{z}\}.
\]

These interactive plots help to explore complex surfaces, especially when detailed inspection of local features is important.

### `surface3d()`: publication-quality 3D surface plots

The generic function `surface3d()` with S3 method `surface3d.qqr()` produces a smooth coloured three-dimensional perspective surface of the raw \(m \times J\) QQR coefficient matrix using base R graphics. It is the R equivalent of MATLAB's `surf()` applied directly to the QQR output, and requires no additional plotting packages.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
surface3d(
  x,
  coef           = x$independent,
  what           = c("coef", "pvalue"),
  palette        = "viridis",
  theta          = -30,
  phi            = 25,
  r              = 3,
  clim           = NULL,
  add_zero_plane = FALSE,
  alpha          = 0.85,
  legend         = TRUE,
  ...
)
```

The horizontal axes span the quantile regressor grid \((z_1,\ldots,z_m)\) and the outcome quantile levels \((\tau_1,\ldots,\tau_J)\), and the vertical axis shows the coefficient or p value at each \((z_i,\tau_j)\). Colour encodes the vertical dimension through a palette from `hcl.colors()`.

Key arguments:

* `coef`: the coefficient to plot. Accepts the quantile regressor name, `"intercept"` or any control variable name.
* `what`: `"coef"` (default) plots the coefficient surface \([\hat\beta_{ij}]\); `"pvalue"` plots the p value surface \([\hat p_{ij}]\).
* `palette`: any palette name accepted by `hcl.colors()`, e.g. `"viridis"`, `"plasma"`, `"RdBu"`, `"YlGnBu"`.
* `theta`, `phi`: azimuthal and colatitudinal viewing angles in degrees, passed to `persp()`.
* `clim`: a two-element numeric vector `c(min, max)` fixing the colour scale limits. Setting this to the same values across multiple plots ensures that colours are directly comparable across coefficients or models.
* `add_zero_plane`: when `TRUE`, a translucent red reference plane at \(z = 0\) is superimposed on the surface. This is particularly useful for coefficient plots, where the zero plane separates positive and negative slopes.
* `alpha`: surface transparency, ranging from 0 (fully transparent) to 1 (fully opaque).
* `legend`: when `TRUE` (the default), a vertical colour scale bar is drawn to the right of the surface.

A typical call for a coefficient surface with zero reference plane:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
surface3d(fit, coef = "X",
          palette        = "RdBu",
          clim           = c(-2, 2),
          add_zero_plane = TRUE,
          theta          = 45,
          phi            = 30)
```

To plot the p value surface:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
surface3d(fit, coef = "X", what = "pvalue",
          clim    = c(0, 1),
          palette = "YlGnBu")
```

### `panel_surface()`: ribbon panel plots

The generic function `panel_surface()` with S3 method `panel_surface.qqr()` produces a ribbon panel plot with one coloured flat panel per coefficient. Panels are arranged side-by-side along the variable axis, with outcome quantile levels on the other axis, and colour encoding coefficient magnitude on a shared scale across all panels. This layout reproduces the style used in several published QQR studies.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
panel_surface(
  x,
  coef           = x$coef_names,
  what           = c("coef", "pvalue"),
  palette        = "viridis",
  theta          = -40,
  phi            = 25,
  clim           = NULL,
  add_zero_plane = FALSE,
  ...
)
```

The `coef` argument accepts a vector of coefficient names, so it is straightforward to display a subset of coefficients. The `clim` argument, shared with `surface3d()`, is especially useful in panel plots because it ensures that colours have the same interpretation across all panels, making direct visual comparison possible.

## Exporting QQR surfaces to external formats

### `excel.qqr()`: Excel workbooks

The function
```{r, eval = FALSE}
excel.qqr(
  x,
  file               = "QQR_coefficients.xlsx",
  which              = c("both", "coef", "pvalue"),
  overwrite          = TRUE,
  include_grid_value = TRUE,
  digits             = NULL
)
```
writes coefficient and p value surfaces to an Excel workbook using `openxlsx`. For each coefficient, the corresponding matrix \([\hat\beta_{ij}]\) or \([\hat p_{ij}]\) is transformed into a data frame with columns
\[
\text{Grid}_{\text{Point}},\quad
\text{Grid}_{\text{Value}},\quad
\tau_{\tau_1},\ldots,\tau_{\tau_J}
\]

mirroring the matrix representation in Section 3.3, and then written to a dedicated worksheet. Sheet names encode the coefficient identity and whether the sheet contains coefficients (`_coef`) or p values (`_pval`). The workbook therefore contains a complete set of tables representing the discrete approximations to \(\alpha(\tau,\theta)\), \(\beta(\tau,\theta)\) and \(\gamma(\tau,\theta)\) and their associated p values.

The `digits` argument allows for rounding of numeric entries in the exported file, while `include_grid_value` controls whether the actual grid values \(z_i\) are included alongside their indices.

### `word.qqr()`: Word documents

The function
```{r, eval = FALSE}
word.qqr(
  x,
  file               = "QQR_results.docx",
  coef               = x$independent,
  which              = c("both", "coef", "pvalue", "coef_stars"),
  grid_subset        = NULL,
  digits             = NULL,
  include_grid_value = TRUE
)
```
exports selected coefficient and p value surfaces to a Word document using `officer` and `flextable`. It begins by extracting the relevant matrices \([\hat\beta_{ij}]\) and \([\hat p_{ij}]\) for the specified coefficient and an optional subset of grid points. Each matrix is converted into a data frame of the form
\[
\text{Grid}_{\text{Point}},\quad
\text{Grid}_{\text{Value}},\quad
\tau_{\tau_1},\ldots,\tau_{\tau_J}
\]
which is then rendered as a formatted table in the Word document.

The `which` argument selects what to export:

* `"coef"`: coefficient table only.
* `"pvalue"`: p value table only.
* `"both"` (default): separate coefficient and p value tables in the same document.
* `"coef_stars"`: a single combined table with significance stars appended directly to each coefficient. This is the format most commonly used in published empirical papers.

When `which = "coef_stars"`, each cell of the table is formatted as
\[
\text{cell}_{ij} =
\hat\beta_{ij} \;\|\;
\begin{cases}
\texttt{***} & \hat p_{ij} < 0.01 \\
\texttt{**}  & \hat p_{ij} < 0.05 \\
\texttt{*}   & \hat p_{ij} < 0.10 \\
             & \hat p_{ij} \ge 0.10 \\
\texttt{[NA]}& \hat p_{ij} = \texttt{NA}
\end{cases}
\]
where `[NA]` marks grid-quantile combinations where p values could not be computed (for example, because the effective local sample size at that grid point was too small). This marker ensures that no cell is left ambiguously blank. A footnote is appended automatically below the table explaining the star conventions and the `[NA]` notation.

As with `excel.qqr()`, rounding via `digits` is applied only at the output stage and does not alter the underlying QQR object.

##  Comparing standard quantile regression with grid-averaged QQR effects

Many applied papers estimate a standard quantile regression (QR) and a quantile-on-quantile regression (QQR) on the same specification and then compare the two sets of coefficients across quantile levels, often using QR as a benchmark because its asymptotic theory is well established and implemented easily (Koenker and Bassett, 1978; Koenker, 2005). QQR is semi-parametric in the sense that the effect of the covariates is allowed to vary smoothly over a grid of quantiles of a chosen regressor and is estimated with local linear quantile regression (Yu and Jones, 1998; Sim and Zhou, 2015). This richer structure yields a full coefficient surface \(\beta(\tau, z)\), indexed by the conditional quantile level \(\tau\) of the response and by the quantile-regressor grid value \(z\).  

Empirically, some researchers treat the formal p-values from QQR with caution because they are obtained from a nonparametric smoothing step and may be sensitive to bandwidth choice, finite-sample bias and boundary effects. They instead check whether the shape of the QQR surface, after an appropriate averaging, is consistent with the simpler QR estimates, which are based on a purely parametric linear conditional quantile model (see Sim and Zhou, 2015, for this robustness check). The `qqrtools` package operationalises this practice by providing tools that collapse the bivariate QQR surface to a univariate function of \(\tau\) and compare it directly with the QR coefficients.

Let \(Y\) denote the response, \(X\) a vector of regressors and \(Z\) the quantile regressor used in QQR (argument `qvar`). A standard linear QR model for a fixed quantile level \(\tau\) assumes  
\[
Q_{Y\mid X}(\tau \mid X = x) = x^{\top}\beta^{\mathrm{QR}}(\tau),
\]
and estimates \(\beta^{\mathrm{QR}}(\tau)\) by minimising the sample check-loss (Koenker, 2005). QQR instead specifies a locally linear model in \(Z\),  
\[
Q_{Y\mid X,Z}(\tau \mid X = x, Z = z)
  = x^{\top}\beta(\tau,z),
\]
where the coefficient vector \(\beta(\tau,z)\) is allowed to vary smoothly in \(z\). In practice, QQR evaluates this surface on a grid of \(M\) values \(z_1,\dots,z_M\) and on a set of quantile levels \(\tau_1,\dots,\tau_K\). For each pair \((\tau_k,z_m)\) a local linear quantile regression is run using kernel weights \(K_h(Z_i - z_m)\) as in Yu and Jones (1998), yielding an estimated surface \(\hat{\beta}(\tau_k,z_m)\).

A natural way to compare QQR with QR is to aggregate \(\hat{\beta}(\tau_k,z_m)\) along the quantile-regressor dimension. Under a stylised data-generating process with continuous \(Z\), if \(Q_{Y\mid X,Z}(\tau\mid X,Z)\) is linear in \(X\) with slope vector \(\beta(\tau,Z)\), and if we define an average conditional quantile model  
\[
Q_{Y\mid X}(\tau \mid X = x)
  := \mathbb{E}\big[Q_{Y\mid X,Z}(\tau \mid X = x, Z) \mid X = x\big],
\]
then, assuming the conditional expectation and quantile operators can be interchanged and that the slope is separable from the distribution of \(Z\),  
\[
Q_{Y\mid X}(\tau \mid X = x) = x^{\top}\,\underbrace{\mathbb{E}[\beta(\tau,Z)]}_{\bar\beta(\tau)}.
\]
In other words, the global QR slope \(\beta^{\mathrm{QR}}(\tau)\) coincides with the average of the QQR slope over the distribution of \(Z\),  
\[
\beta^{\mathrm{QR}}(\tau) = \bar\beta(\tau)
= \int \beta(\tau,z)\, f_Z(z)\,\mathrm{d}z,
\]
where \(f_Z\) is the density of \(Z\).  

In the QQR implementation, \(f_Z\) is approximated by the empirical distribution of the grid points \(z_m\). With the default quantile grid (`grid = "quantile"`), the points \(z_m = \hat Q_Z(\theta_m)\) at equally spaced \(\theta_m\) represent the distribution of \(Z\), so the equally weighted average is a Riemann approximation to the integral (Sim and Zhou, 2015). With `grid = "range"` the average weights the range of \(Z\) uniformly instead, and `compare.qqr()` prints a message. The grid-averaged QQR effect at quantile \(\tau_k\) is  
\[
\hat{\bar\beta}(\tau_k)
  = \frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M} \hat{\beta}(\tau_k,z_m).
\]
If the QQR surface is a consistent estimator of \(\beta(\tau,z)\) and the grid covers the support of \(Z\), then \(\hat{\bar\beta}(\tau_k)\) converges to the same limit as the QR slope \(\hat{\beta}^{\mathrm{QR}}(\tau_k)\) under the model described above. The comparison  
\[
\hat{\beta}^{\mathrm{QR}}(\tau_k) \quad\text{versus}\quad \hat{\bar\beta}(\tau_k)
\]
becomes a diagnostic for whether the more flexible QQR surface, once averaged over the quantiles of the regressor, behaves consistently with the simpler QR model. Large discrepancies suggest either that the QQR surface captures richer nonlinearity or interaction that the global QR cannot see, or that the smoothing and bandwidth choices in QQR are inducing non-negligible bias.  

The `qqrtools` package provides a family of helper functions that automate this comparison:

- `compare.qqr()` constructs a tidy data frame with the QR coefficients and grid-averaged QQR effects for a chosen coefficient across the \(\tau\) values of the fit.
- `excel.compare.qqr()` exports the same comparison table to an Excel workbook using `openxlsx`.
- `word.compare.qqr()` exports the comparison table as a formatted Word document using `officer` and `flextable`.
- `plot.compare.qqr()` is a plotting method for the comparison object that produces publication-ready coefficient plots with \(\tau\) on the horizontal axis and coefficient values on the vertical axis using `ggplot2`.

The following subsections explain each function in detail and illustrate how they can be used in empirical work.

###  Comparing QR and grid-averaged QQR with `compare.qqr()`

The function `compare.qqr()` takes an object produced by `qqr()` and quietly fits a standard QR with the same formula, dataset and set of quantile levels. It then aggregates the QQR coefficient surface across the quantile-regressor grid and returns a tidy table with one row per quantile level \(\tau\).  

Conceptually, `compare.qqr()` implements the mapping  
\[
(\hat{\beta}^{\mathrm{QR}}(\tau_k),\; \hat{\beta}(\tau_k,z_1),\dots,\hat{\beta}(\tau_k,z_M))
     \;\longmapsto\;
(\tau_k,\;\hat{\beta}^{\mathrm{QR}}(\tau_k),\;\hat{\bar\beta}(\tau_k)),
\]
where \(\hat{\bar\beta}(\tau_k)\) is the grid-average QQR effect defined above. The function focuses on a single coefficient at a time, typically the quantile regressor itself or a key control.  

At a high level the interface is

```r
compare.qqr(x,
            coef   = x$independent,
            na.rm  = TRUE,
            digits = NULL)
```

The arguments are:

- `x`: a fitted QQR object produced by `qqr()`.
- `coef`: a character vector with the coefficients to compare. The default is `x$independent` (the quantile regressor). Use `"all"` to compare all coefficients, or provide one or more specific names such as `"intercept"`, `"(Intercept)"` or control-variable names.
- `na.rm`: logical flag passed to the averaging step. When `TRUE` (the default), missing entries in the QQR surface are removed before averaging over the grid.
- `digits`: optional integer controlling the rounding of both QR and averaged QQR coefficients in the returned table. Rounding is purely cosmetic and does not alter the underlying fits.

When a single coefficient is requested, `compare.qqr()` returns a data frame with four columns:

- `tau`: the quantile level \(\tau_k\);
- `qr`: the QR coefficient \(\hat{\beta}^{\mathrm{QR}}(\tau_k)\);
- `qqr_mean`: the grid-averaged QQR coefficient \(\hat{\bar\beta}(\tau_k)\) (the column mean of the surface);
- `difference`: `qqr_mean - qr`.

For the intercept the two columns are not directly comparable: the local intercept is the fitted \(\tau\)-quantile of \(Y\) at \(Z = z_m\), whereas the QR intercept refers to \(Z = 0\).

When multiple coefficients are requested, the function returns a named list of such data frames, with one element per coefficient. This format is convenient for exporting and plotting coefficient-specific comparisons.

For example, continuing the simulated example in Section 5 below, one could write

```r
cmp_X <- compare.qqr(fit, coef = "X", digits = 3)
head(cmp_X)
```

which produces a table suitable for direct inclusion in a report or for further processing by the export and plotting helpers described next.

###  Exporting QR-QQR comparisons to Excel with `excel.compare.qqr()`

The function `excel.compare.qqr()` wraps `compare.qqr()` and writes its output to an Excel workbook using `openxlsx`. This is useful when QR--QQR comparisons need to be archived, shared with collaborators or imported into other software. The typical call is

```r
excel.compare.qqr(
  x,
  file   = "QQR_QR_comparison.xlsx",
  coef   = x$independent,
  na.rm  = TRUE,
  digits = NULL
)
```

The arguments mirror those of `compare.qqr()` with one additional parameter:

- `file`: path to the Excel file to be created. If a file with the same name already exists, it is overwritten by default (the behaviour of `openxlsx::saveWorkbook()` in this wrapper).

If `coef` identifies a single coefficient, the resulting workbook contains one worksheet with three columns (`tau`, `qr`, `qqr_mean`). If `coef = "all"` or a vector of names is supplied, each coefficient is written to its own worksheet, whose name encodes the coefficient label. The exported tables preserve the one-row-per-quantile structure and the ordering of \(\tau\) values used in the original QQR fit.

### Exporting QR-QQR comparisons to Word with `word.compare.qqr()`

For users who prepare documents in Word, `word.compare.qqr()` provides an analogous export facility using the `officer` and `flextable` packages. It takes the same core arguments as `compare.qqr()`:

```r
word.compare.qqr(
  x,
  file   = "QQR_QR_comparison.docx",
  coef   = x$independent,
  na.rm  = TRUE,
  digits = NULL
)
```

For each requested coefficient, the function inserts a short heading indicating the dependent variable and coefficient name, followed by a `flextable` with the columns `tau`, `qr`, `qqr_mean` and `difference`. These tables use the same ordering and rounding as the output of `compare.qqr()`. The resulting document can be edited further in Word, for example by adjusting table styles, adding captions or combining the comparisons with narrative interpretation.

This helper is especially convenient when QR--QQR robustness checks are reported as separate tables in empirical papers, for example to demonstrate that the averaged QQR effects track the standard QR coefficients for key regressors.

###  Plotting QR and grid-averaged QQR coefficients with `plot.compare.qqr()`

Visual comparison of QR and QQR is often more informative than inspection of tables alone. The S3 method `plot.compare.qqr()` constructs a two-line coefficient plot using `ggplot2`, with quantile levels on the horizontal axis and coefficient values on the vertical axis. Its interface is

```r
## S3 method for class 'compare.qqr'
plot(
  x,
  coef         = x$independent,
  title        = NULL,
  xlab         = "Quantile level (tau)",
  ylab         = "Coefficient",
  legend_title = "",
  na.rm        = TRUE,
  digits       = NULL
)
```

Here:

- `x` is typically the original `qqr` fit. Internally, the method calls `compare.qqr()` to obtain the comparison table for the requested coefficient.
- `coef` selects the coefficient to plot. Only a single coefficient is allowed. The default is the quantile regressor.
- `title` is an optional plot title. When `NULL`, a default title is constructed using the coefficient name and the dependent variable.
- `xlab`, `ylab` and `legend_title` control the axis and legend labels.
- `na.rm` and `digits` are passed through to `compare.qqr()` to control the treatment of missing values and rounding before plotting.

The method returns a `ggplot` object, so users can further customise the theme or layers. A typical usage pattern is

```r
## Compare QR and QQR for the quantile regressor
p_X <- plot.compare.qqr(fit, coef = "X")
p_X
```

which draws a plot with the QR coefficients and row--mean QQR coefficients connected by lines across \(\tau\). Discrepancies between the two lines highlight quantile regions where the nonparametric QQR reveals behaviour that is not captured by the global linear QR model.

##  Two-dimensional static and interactive visualisation

The functions described in this section provide a comprehensive second layer of
visualisation tools that complement the three-dimensional surfaces introduced
in Section 4.4. Where `surface3d()`, `panel_surface()`, `plot.qqr()` and
`Int.plot()` render the coefficient matrix as a perspective surface in
\(\mathbb{R}^3\), the four functions introduced here approach the same
\(m \times J\) matrix from a different angle: they map it directly into the
two-dimensional joint quantile plane \((z_i, \tau_j)\), using colour
or iso-lines to encode the coefficient value. This representation has three
practical advantages for publication.

First, every cell of the surface is visible simultaneously and unambiguously.
In a perspective rendering, parts of the surface that face away from the viewer
are hidden. In a two-dimensional heatmap or contour plot, nothing is occluded.

Second, the figures are resolution-independent in print. A heatmap or contour
plot renders identically at 72 dpi on screen and at 600 dpi in a journal
submission, whereas the visual impression of a perspective surface changes
with resolution and viewing angle.

Third, the zero contour — the boundary where \(\hat\beta_{ij} = 0\) — can be
drawn explicitly and precisely as a curve in the joint quantile plane, making
it straightforward to identify the exact quantile combinations at which the
direction of the effect reverses. In a 3D surface this boundary is the
intersection of the surface with a horizontal plane, which can be difficult to
read from a two-dimensional reproduction of a three-dimensional rendering.

Taken together, the four functions form a logical pair of pairs. The static
ggplot2 functions `qqr_heatmap()` and `qqr_contour()` are intended for
journal figures and manuscript drafts; the interactive plotly function
`qqr_plotly()` is intended for exploratory analysis and online supplementary
material; and the pre-estimation function `qqr_cor_heatmap()` is intended for
the exploratory step that precedes model fitting.

### `qqr_heatmap()`: publication-ready two-dimensional heatmaps

The function

```{r, eval = FALSE}
qqr_heatmap(
  x,
  coef         = NULL,
  what         = c("coef", "pvalue"),
  palette      = "RdBu",
  center_zero  = NULL,
  clim         = NULL,
  sig_overlay  = c("none", "stars", "dots"),
  sig_levels   = c("***" = 0.01, "**" = 0.05, "*" = 0.10),
  sig_size     = 2.8,
  sig_colour   = "black",
  grid_values  = TRUE,
  xlab         = NULL,
  ylab         = NULL,
  title        = NULL,
  digits       = 2L,
  ...
)
```

produces a publication-ready two-dimensional heatmap of the QQR coefficient
or p-value surface using `ggplot2`. Each cell at position \((z_i, \tau_j)\)
is filled with a colour that encodes \(\hat\beta_{ij}\) or \(\hat p_{ij}\)
respectively. The function returns a `ggplot2` object, which can be printed
directly, modified with additional `ggplot2` layers, or saved with
`ggplot2::ggsave()`.

**Mathematical representation.** Let \(\mathbf{B}\) denote the \(m \times J\)
matrix with \((\mathbf{B})_{ij} = \hat\beta_{ij}\), where \(i = 1,\ldots,m\)
indexes the quantile-regressor grid and \(j = 1,\ldots,J\) indexes the
outcome quantile levels. The heatmap renders the mapping
\[
(z_i,\, \tau_j) \;\longmapsto\; \hat\beta_{ij}
\]
as a colour-coded grid in the plane, with the horizontal axis corresponding
to \(\tau_j\) and the vertical axis to \(z_i\). This is the same mathematical
object as the coefficient surface in Section 3.3, collapsed from
\(\mathbb{R}^3\) to a colour channel.

**Colour scaling.** The default palette `"RdBu"` maps negative coefficients
to blue and positive coefficients to red, with white at the midpoint. When
`center_zero = TRUE`, the colour midpoint is pinned to exactly
\(\hat\beta = 0\), so the white boundary in the plot identifies the contour
\(\{(z_i, \tau_j) : \hat\beta_{ij} \approx 0\}\) — the same zero contour
that `qqr_contour()` draws explicitly as a line. This is automatic when a
diverging palette is selected with `what = "coef"`. For p-value surfaces,
`center_zero` defaults to `FALSE` because the natural range is \([0, 1]\)
rather than \([-1, 1]\).

When multiple models are to be compared visually, `clim = c(min, max)` fixes
the colour limits so that a given colour carries the same coefficient value
in every figure. Without a fixed scale, each figure uses its own data range
and colours are not comparable across plots.

**Significance overlay.** The `sig_overlay` argument adds symbols to
significant cells using the p-value surface stored in the fitted QQR object.
Setting `sig_overlay = "stars"` prints the strings `"***"`, `"**"` or
`"*"` inside each cell that passes the corresponding threshold in
`sig_levels`. Setting `sig_overlay = "dots"` prints a filled bullet
character (\(\bullet\)) instead. The overlay requires that the model was
fitted with `se_type != "none"` so that p-value surfaces exist.

Formally, a cell \((z_i, \tau_j)\) receives a label of `"***"` if and only
if \(\hat p_{ij} < 0.01\), of `"**"` if \(0.01 \le \hat p_{ij} < 0.05\),
and of `"*"` if \(0.05 \le \hat p_{ij} < 0.10\). Cells with
\(\hat p_{ij} \ge 0.10\) or with \(\hat p_{ij} = \texttt{NA}\) carry no
overlay.

**Multi-coefficient faceting.** Setting `coef = "all"` invokes
`ggplot2::facet_wrap()` to produce one panel per coefficient in a single
figure. All panels share the same colour scale, so the magnitudes of
intercept, quantile regressor and control variable effects are directly
comparable. This reproduces, in two dimensions, the layout of
`panel_surface()` and is often more suitable for print publication.

The key arguments are:

- `x`: a fitted QQR object produced by `qqr()`.
- `coef`: the coefficient to plot. Accepts the quantile regressor name,
  `"intercept"`, `"(Intercept)"`, any control name, or `"all"` for
  a faceted figure.
- `what`: `"coef"` (default) plots \([\hat\beta_{ij}]\); `"pvalue"` plots
  \([\hat p_{ij}]\).
- `palette`: any `RColorBrewer` palette name. Diverging palettes such as
  `"RdBu"`, `"BrBG"` and `"PuOr"` are recommended for coefficient surfaces;
  sequential palettes such as `"YlOrRd"` or `"Plasma"` are recommended for
  p-value surfaces.
- `center_zero`: logical; if `TRUE` the colour midpoint is fixed at zero.
  Defaults to `TRUE` when `what = "coef"` and a diverging palette is used.
- `clim`: a numeric vector `c(min, max)` fixing the colour limits.
  Essential for cross-model comparison.
- `sig_overlay`: `"none"` (default), `"stars"`, or `"dots"`.
- `sig_levels`: named numeric vector of p-value thresholds for stars.
  Default is `c("***" = 0.01, "**" = 0.05, "*" = 0.10)`.
- `grid_values`: if `TRUE` (default), the vertical axis shows the actual
  sample quantile values \(z_i\) of the quantile regressor at each grid
  point. If `FALSE`, the integer grid index \(i\) is shown instead.

A typical call for a coefficient heatmap with significance stars:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
p_heatmap <- qqr_heatmap(
  fit,
  coef        = "X",
  palette     = "RdBu",
  center_zero = TRUE,
  sig_overlay = "stars",
  grid_values = TRUE,
  title       = "QQR coefficient surface: X on Y"
)

p_heatmap

## Save at publication resolution
ggplot2::ggsave("heatmap_X.png", p_heatmap, width = 9, height = 6, dpi = 300)
```

To fix the colour scale for a cross-model comparison between, say, a
forward transmission model and a reverse transmission model fitted to the same
data:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## Forward: X -> Y
p_fwd <- qqr_heatmap(fit_fwd, coef = "X", clim = c(-0.5, 0.5),
                      center_zero = TRUE, sig_overlay = "stars")

## Reverse: Y -> X   (directional asymmetry check)
p_rev <- qqr_heatmap(fit_rev, coef = "Y", clim = c(-0.5, 0.5),
                      center_zero = TRUE, sig_overlay = "stars")
```

The identical `clim` argument ensures that a given shade of red or blue
represents the same coefficient value in both figures, making the
directional comparison valid.

To display all coefficients simultaneously on a shared scale:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## Faceted heatmap: intercept, quantile regressor and all controls
p_all <- qqr_heatmap(
  fit,
  coef        = "all",
  palette     = "RdBu",
  center_zero = TRUE,
  sig_overlay = "stars"
)

ggplot2::ggsave("heatmap_all_coef.png", p_all, width = 16, height = 6,
                dpi = 300)
```

###  `qqr_contour()`: publication-ready contour plots

The function

```{r, eval = FALSE}
qqr_contour(
  x,
  coef          = NULL,
  what          = c("coef", "pvalue"),
  filled        = TRUE,
  n_levels      = 10L,
  palette       = "RdBu",
  center_zero   = NULL,
  clim          = NULL,
  zero_contour  = TRUE,
  zero_lwd      = 1.2,
  sig_mask      = FALSE,
  sig_threshold = 0.10,
  grid_values   = TRUE,
  xlab          = NULL,
  ylab          = NULL,
  title         = NULL,
  digits        = 2L,
  ...
)
```

produces a two-dimensional contour plot of a single QQR coefficient or
p-value surface using `ggplot2`. Contour lines connect cells of equal
coefficient value in the joint quantile plane, and optional filled colour
bands shade the regions between successive iso-lines. The function returns
a `ggplot2` object.

**Mathematical representation.** A contour line at height \(c\) is the
level set
\[
\mathcal{L}(c)
=
\{(z, \tau) \in [z_1, z_m] \times [\tau_1, \tau_J]
   : \hat\beta(z, \tau) = c\},
\]
where \(\hat\beta(z, \tau)\) denotes the bicubically interpolated
coefficient surface obtained from the discrete estimates \(\hat\beta_{ij}\).
Internally, the function passes the \(m \times J\) matrix
\([\hat\beta_{ij}]\) to `ggplot2::geom_contour_filled()`, which computes
these level sets on a fine internal grid using the CONREC algorithm.
This is the methodologically correct approach. An earlier implementation in
the literature (Roudane, 2026) passed raw coefficient vectors directly to
a plotly contour trace, which produced unreliable level sets; passing the
full matrix avoids that problem.

**Zero contour.** When `zero_contour = TRUE` (the default) and zero lies
within the data range, a bold black line is drawn at
\(\hat\beta(z, \tau) = 0\) on top of the filled bands. This line has
immediate economic interpretation: it marks the boundary between quantile
combinations at which the effect of the regressor is positive and those
at which it is negative. Setting `zero_lwd` controls the line width;
the default of 1.2 is heavier than the thin grey iso-lines at other
levels so that the zero contour stands out clearly.

**Significance mask.** When `sig_mask = TRUE`, a semi-transparent grey
rectangle is drawn over every cell \((z_i, \tau_j)\) for which the
stored p-value satisfies \(\hat p_{ij} > \texttt{sig\_threshold}\). This
overlay directs the reader's attention to the statistically supported region
of the surface. Cells that are masked are not necessarily zero; they are
