cells for which the evidence against the null hypothesis \(\beta = 0\) is
weak given the chosen threshold. The mask requires that the model was
fitted with `se_type != "none"`.

The key arguments are:

- `x`: a fitted QQR object.
- `coef`: the coefficient to plot. One coefficient at a time; for multiple
  coefficients call the function separately.
- `what`: `"coef"` (default) or `"pvalue"`.
- `filled`: if `TRUE` (default), filled colour bands are drawn between
  the iso-lines using `geom_contour_filled()`. If `FALSE`, line contours
  only are drawn using `geom_contour()`.
- `n_levels`: the number of contour levels. The break points are placed
  at equal intervals between `clim[1]` and `clim[2]`, or between the
  observed minimum and maximum when `clim = NULL`.
- `palette`: any `RColorBrewer` palette name, matched to the choice for
  `qqr_heatmap()` to ensure visual consistency within a paper.
- `center_zero`: see `qqr_heatmap()`. The same logic applies.
- `zero_contour`: if `TRUE` (default) and zero is in the data range,
  a bold black iso-line at \(\hat\beta = 0\) is superimposed.
- `zero_lwd`: line width of the zero contour.
- `sig_mask`: if `TRUE`, grey shading is drawn over non-significant cells.
- `sig_threshold`: the p-value cutoff for the significance mask.
- `grid_values`: same as in `qqr_heatmap()`.

A typical call for a coefficient contour with the zero iso-line and a
ten percent significance mask:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
p_contour <- qqr_contour(
  fit,
  coef          = "X",
  filled        = TRUE,
  n_levels      = 10L,
  palette       = "RdBu",
  center_zero   = TRUE,
  zero_contour  = TRUE,
  sig_mask      = TRUE,
  sig_threshold = 0.10,
  grid_values   = TRUE,
  title         = "QQR contour: X on Y  [grey = p > 10%]"
)

p_contour

ggplot2::ggsave("contour_X.png", p_contour, width = 9, height = 6, dpi = 300)
```

For a line-only contour without fill, which is sometimes preferred in
grey-scale journals:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
p_contour_lines <- qqr_contour(
  fit,
  coef         = "X",
  filled       = FALSE,
  n_levels     = 12L,
  palette      = "RdBu",
  center_zero  = TRUE,
  zero_contour = TRUE,
  grid_values  = TRUE
)
```

As with `qqr_heatmap()`, setting `clim` to a common vector across two
models places their zero contours at the same absolute coefficient value and
makes the comparison geometrically meaningful.

###  `qqr_plotly()`: unified interactive visualisation hub

The function

```{r, eval = FALSE}
qqr_plotly(
  x,
  coef               = NULL,
  what               = c("coef", "pvalue"),
  type               = c("surface", "heatmap", "contour"),
  colorscale         = "Viridis",
  clim               = NULL,
  center_zero        = NULL,
  show_zero_plane    = FALSE,
  zero_plane_opacity = 0.25,
  show_contour       = TRUE,
  n_contours         = 10L,
  show_labels        = TRUE,
  sig_overlay        = FALSE,
  sig_threshold      = 0.05,
  sig_symbol         = "*",
  grid_values        = TRUE,
  aspect_ratio       = c(1, 1, 0.7),
  camera             = list(eye = list(x = 1.4, y = 1.7, z = 1.2)),
  xlab               = NULL,
  ylab               = NULL,
  title              = NULL,
  digits             = 2L,
  ...
)
```

is a unified interactive visualisation hub that produces three display
types from a single entry point, controlled by the `type` argument.
All types return a `plotly` object that can be displayed in the RStudio
Viewer pane, embedded in an R Markdown document or saved as a
self-contained HTML file. The function requires `plotly` to be installed
and gives an informative error message if it is not.

This design deliberately consolidates the three separate plotly functions
in Roudane (2026) into one consistent interface. All types share the same
data extraction pipeline from the `qqr` object, the same colour scale
logic and the same hover tooltip that displays the actual grid value
\(z_i\), the quantile level \(\tau_j\) and the coefficient or p-value at
each cell. Earlier implementations that passed only row or column indices
to the hover template produced tooltips that required the reader to
cross-reference a separate grid table; here the actual values are embedded
directly.

**`type = "surface"`: interactive three-dimensional surface.**
The coefficient matrix \([\hat\beta_{ij}]\) is passed as a
\(\tau\)-by-\(z\) grid to `plotly::plot_ly()` with `type = "surface"`.
The resulting plot can be rotated, zoomed and panned in the viewer. The
`camera` argument sets the initial viewpoint; `aspect_ratio` controls the
proportions of the three axes; and `show_contour = TRUE` draws grid lines
on the surface to help the eye track the grid coordinates.

When `show_zero_plane = TRUE`, a second semi-transparent surface is added
at height \(\hat\beta = 0\), corresponding to the plane
\(\{(z, \tau, \hat\beta) : \hat\beta = 0\}\).
This is the interactive counterpart of the `add_zero_plane` option in
`surface3d()`. The opacity of the zero plane is controlled by
`zero_plane_opacity`.

**`type = "heatmap"`: interactive two-dimensional heatmap.**
The coefficient matrix is rendered as a plotly heatmap trace. Every cell
carries a hover tooltip showing the precise coefficient value, making the
interactive heatmap complementary to the static `qqr_heatmap()`: the static
version is suitable for print, while the interactive version allows the
reader to interrogate individual cells without referring to separate tables.

When `sig_overlay = TRUE`, star annotations are added to cells where
\(\hat p_{ij} < \texttt{sig\_threshold}\). The annotation symbol is
controlled by `sig_symbol` and defaults to `"*"`.

**`type = "contour"`: interactive two-dimensional contour.**
The coefficient matrix is rendered as a plotly contour trace. The
`n_contours` argument sets the number of levels and `show_labels = TRUE`
prints the coefficient value alongside each iso-line in the interactive
figure. A separate heavy black contour trace is added automatically at
\(\hat\beta = 0\) when zero lies in the data range, matching the
`zero_contour` behaviour in `qqr_contour()`.

The key arguments common to all three types:

- `x`: a fitted QQR object.
- `coef`: the coefficient to visualise. One coefficient at a time.
- `what`: `"coef"` (default) or `"pvalue"`.
- `type`: `"surface"` (default), `"heatmap"` or `"contour"`.
- `colorscale`: a plotly colour scale name or a list of `[position, colour]`
  pairs. Passing `"RdBu"` automatically constructs a proper diverging list
  because plotly does not accept `"RdBu"` as a string for surface traces.
- `clim`: `c(min, max)` fixing the colour and z limits.
- `center_zero`: pin the colour midpoint to zero. Auto-detected from
  `colorscale` and `what`.
- `grid_values`: controls whether axis ticks and hover tooltips show actual
  \(z_i\) values or grid indices.

Type-specific arguments are documented further in the function's help page.

A typical exploratory workflow uses all three types in sequence:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## Interactive 3D surface with zero plane
p_surf <- qqr_plotly(
  fit,
  coef             = "X",
  type             = "surface",
  colorscale       = "Viridis",
  show_zero_plane  = TRUE,
  zero_plane_opacity = 0.20,
  show_contour     = TRUE
)
p_surf

## Interactive heatmap with significance overlay
p_heat <- qqr_plotly(
  fit,
  coef           = "X",
  type           = "heatmap",
  colorscale     = "RdBu",
  center_zero    = TRUE,
  sig_overlay    = TRUE,
  sig_threshold  = 0.05
)
p_heat

## Interactive contour
p_con <- qqr_plotly(
  fit,
  coef        = "X",
  type        = "contour",
  colorscale  = "RdBu",
  center_zero = TRUE,
  n_contours  = 12L,
  show_labels = TRUE
)
p_con
```

To save any of the three types as a self-contained HTML file suitable for
online supplementary material:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## Requires the htmlwidgets package
htmlwidgets::saveWidget(p_surf, "QQR_surface_interactive.html",
                        selfcontained = TRUE)
htmlwidgets::saveWidget(p_heat, "QQR_heatmap_interactive.html",
                        selfcontained = TRUE)
htmlwidgets::saveWidget(p_con,  "QQR_contour_interactive.html",
                        selfcontained = TRUE)
```

The self-contained files bundle all JavaScript dependencies and can be
opened in any modern browser without an internet connection.

### `qqr_cor_heatmap()`: pre-estimation quantile dependence heatmap

The function

```{r, eval = FALSE}
qqr_cor_heatmap(
  x,
  method             = c("spearman", "kendall", "somers_d",
                          "pearson", "blomqvist", "coexceedance"),
  mode               = c("subsample", "binary"),
  n_bins             = NULL,
  palette            = NULL,
  center_zero        = NULL,
  clim               = NULL,
  annotate           = TRUE,
  ann_size           = 2.6,
  ann_thresh         = 0.55,
  independence_line  = TRUE,
  grid_values        = TRUE,
  xlab               = NULL,
  ylab               = NULL,
  title              = NULL,
  subtitle           = NULL,
  digits             = 2L,
  min_cell_n         = 3L,
  ...
)
```

is fundamentally different from the three visualisation functions described
above: it is a **pre-estimation diagnostic** that uses only the raw data
stored in `x$data` and does not depend on the estimated QQR surfaces. Its
purpose is to characterise the bivariate dependence structure between
the dependent variable \(Y\) and the quantile regressor \(X\) across the
joint quantile plane \emph{before} any model is fitted, and thereby to provide
statistical justification for proceeding with QQR rather than standard QR.

The function returns a named list of class `"qqr_cor_heatmap"` with elements:

- `$plot`: the `ggplot2` object.
- `$matrix`: the \(n_{\text{bins}} \times n_{\text{bins}}\) numeric
  matrix of dependence values.
- `$cell_n`: the integer matrix of observation counts per cell
  (for `mode = "subsample"`).
- `$x_breaks`, `$y_breaks`: the quantile threshold vectors defining the
  bin boundaries.
- `$method`, `$mode`: the method and mode used.

A `print` method summarises the range, mean and number of `NA` cells.

**Motivation.** Standard QR assumes a linear model in which the slope of
\(X\) on the \(\tau\)-quantile of \(Y\) is a function of \(\tau\) alone.
If that slope also varies with the quantile state of \(X\) itself, then the
conditional dependence between \(X\) and \(Y\) is heterogeneous across the
joint support of \((X, Y)\). The `qqr_cor_heatmap()` function tests for this
heterogeneity directly. A heatmap that is approximately uniform across cells
suggests that QR is adequate. A heatmap that varies substantially — especially
one that changes sign from the lower-left to the upper-right corner of the
plot — provides non-parametric evidence that QQR is warranted.

**Computation modes.** The `mode` argument selects the computation strategy.

In `mode = "subsample"` (recommended), the data are partitioned into
\(n_{\text{bins}} \times n_{\text{bins}}\) non-overlapping cells by jointly
binning \(X\) and \(Y\) at their respective empirical quantile thresholds.
The chosen dependence measure is then computed on the observations that fall
within each cell using their actual continuous values. Formally, define the
cell boundaries
\[
a_i = \hat{Q}_X\!\left(\tfrac{i-1}{n_{\text{bins}}}\right),
\quad
b_i = \hat{Q}_X\!\left(\tfrac{i}{n_{\text{bins}}}\right),
\quad i = 1,\ldots,n_{\text{bins}},
\]
and analogously for \(Y\). The cell \((i, j)\) contains the observations
\[
\mathcal{C}_{ij}
=
\{t : X_t \in (a_i, b_i],\; Y_t \in (c_j, d_j]\},
\]
and the statistic for that cell is computed from \(\{(X_t, Y_t) : t \in \mathcal{C}_{ij}\}\). Cells with fewer than `min_cell_n` observations return `NA` and are displayed in grey.

In `mode = "binary"`, the function replicates the approach of Roudane (2026):
for each pair of thresholds \((Q_X(\tau_i), Q_Y(\tau_j))\), the correlation
between the binary indicators \(\mathbf{1}[X_t \le Q_X(\tau_i)]\) and
\(\mathbf{1}[Y_t \le Q_Y(\tau_j)]\) is computed across the full sample.
This mode is retained for reproducibility and citation but is methodologically
weaker than the subsample mode because binary indicators discard all
within-cell variation; the subsample mode should be preferred in practice.
The binary mode is valid only for `method` values that accept 0/1 data:
`"spearman"`, `"kendall"` and `"pearson"`. Requesting `"somers_d"`,
`"blomqvist"` or `"coexceedance"` with `mode = "binary"` triggers an
automatic switch to `"subsample"` with a warning.

**Six dependence measures.** The `method` argument selects the statistic
computed within each cell.

*Spearman rank correlation* (`"spearman"`) is the default. It measures
monotonic association using ranks and is robust to outliers and non-normality.
For cell \((i, j)\) containing \(n_{ij}\) observations, the Spearman
correlation is
\[
\rho_{ij}^S
=
1 - \frac{6 \sum_{t \in \mathcal{C}_{ij}}
           (R_t^X - R_t^Y)^2}{n_{ij}(n_{ij}^2 - 1)},
\]
where \(R_t^X\) and \(R_t^Y\) are the ranks of \(X_t\) and \(Y_t\) within
the cell. The range is \([-1, 1]\).

*Kendall's \(\tau_b\)* (`"kendall"`) measures concordance relative to all
pairs within the cell:
\[
\tau_{b,ij}
=
\frac{C_{ij} - D_{ij}}
{\sqrt{(C_{ij} + D_{ij} + T_{X,ij})(C_{ij} + D_{ij} + T_{Y,ij})}},
\]
where \(C_{ij}\), \(D_{ij}\), \(T_{X,ij}\) and \(T_{Y,ij}\) are the
numbers of concordant pairs, discordant pairs, pairs tied on \(X\) and pairs
tied on \(Y\) respectively. Kendall's \(\tau_b\) tends to be more robust
than Spearman when cell sample sizes are small or when many observations
share the same value.

*Somers' \(D(Y|X)\)* (`"somers_d"`) is an asymmetric rank association
measure defined as
\[
D_{ij}(Y \mid X)
=
\frac{C_{ij} - D_{ij}}{C_{ij} + D_{ij} + T^{*}_{Y,ij}},
\]
where \(T^{*}_{Y,ij}\) is the number of pairs tied on \(Y\) but not on
\(X\), so that the denominator counts all pairs whose \(X\) values
differ (Somers, 1962). Because \(D(Y|X) \neq D(X|Y)\), Somers'
D is directional — it measures the degree to which knowing that one unit
has a higher \(X\) value than another predicts that the same unit also has
a higher \(Y\) value. This asymmetry directly mirrors QQR's own structure,
in which \(X\) is designated as the predictor of \(Y\) and not conversely.
For this reason, Somers' D is the recommended default for QQR pre-estimation
diagnostics. The range is \([-1, 1]\).

*Pearson linear correlation* (`"pearson"`) computes the standard product-moment
correlation within each cell:
\[
r_{ij}
=
\frac{\sum_{t \in \mathcal{C}_{ij}} (X_t - \bar X_{ij})(Y_t - \bar Y_{ij})}
{\sqrt{\sum_{t} (X_t - \bar X_{ij})^2 \sum_{t} (Y_t - \bar Y_{ij})^2}}.
\]
It is included as a familiar linear baseline but is more sensitive than rank
measures to the distribution of values within each cell and to the assumption
of approximate linearity within the subsample.

*Blomqvist's \(\beta\)* (`"blomqvist"`) is the medial or sign correlation,
defined as the proportion of observations concordant with the cell medians
minus the proportion discordant:
\[
\beta_{ij}
=
\frac{n_{ij}^{++} + n_{ij}^{--} - n_{ij}^{+-} - n_{ij}^{-+}}{n_{ij}^{++} + n_{ij}^{--} + n_{ij}^{+-} + n_{ij}^{-+}},
\]
where \(n_{ij}^{++}\) counts observations with both \(X_t > \tilde X_{ij}\)
and \(Y_t > \tilde Y_{ij}\) (and analogously for the other quadrants),
with \(\tilde X_{ij}\) and \(\tilde Y_{ij}\) denoting the within-cell
medians. Because Blomqvist's \(\beta\) uses only the sign of deviations from
the cell median and not their magnitude, it is extremely robust to outliers
and to small cell sample sizes, which makes it particularly well-suited to
QQR pre-estimation where cells in the corners of the quantile grid often
contain only a handful of observations. The range is \([-1, 1]\).

*Co-exceedance probability* (`"coexceedance"`) is defined as
\[
p_{ij}
=
\frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T}
\mathbf{1}\!\left[X_t \ge \hat Q_X\!\left(\tfrac{i-1}{n_{\text{bins}}}\right)\right]
\mathbf{1}\!\left[Y_t \ge \hat Q_Y\!\left(\tfrac{j-1}{n_{\text{bins}}}\right)\right],
\]
which is the empirical proportion of observations that jointly exceed both
lower bin boundaries. Under independence, this probability equals
\((1 - \tau_i)(1 - \tau_j)\), where \(\tau_i = (i-1)/n_{\text{bins}}\) and
\(\tau_j = (j-1)/n_{\text{bins}}\) are the lower-boundary quantile levels.
Values exceeding \((1 - \tau_i)(1 - \tau_j)\) indicate positive tail
dependence, meaning that \(X\) and \(Y\) tend to be jointly large more
often than independence would predict. This measure is the most widely used
tail-dependence statistic in the financial contagion and uncertainty
transmission literature and is a natural complement to QQR when the research
question concerns joint extreme events. Setting `independence_line = TRUE`
(the default for this method) draws the independence benchmark
\((1 - \tau_i)(1 - \tau_j)\) as a dashed contour superimposed on the heatmap.
The range is \([0, 1]\). For this method, `palette` defaults to `"YlOrRd"`
(a sequential yellow-to-red scale) and `center_zero` defaults to `FALSE`.

**Grid alignment.** By default, `n_bins` is set to `length(x$taus)`, the
number of quantile levels used in the QQR fit. This ensures that the
pre-estimation heatmap and the post-estimation `qqr_heatmap()` output have
the same grid dimensions and can be placed side by side for direct visual
comparison.

The key arguments are:

- `x`: a fitted QQR object. Only `x$data`, `x$independent`, `x$dependent`
  and `x$taus` are used; the estimated surfaces are ignored.
- `method`: the dependence statistic; see above. The recommended choice for
  QQR pre-estimation is `"somers_d"`.
- `mode`: `"subsample"` (recommended) or `"binary"` (Roudane, 2026).
- `n_bins`: number of quantile bins per axis. Default: `length(x$taus)`.
- `annotate`: if `TRUE` (default), the numeric value of the dependence
  statistic is printed inside each cell.
- `independence_line`: for `method = "coexceedance"` only; draws the
  independence benchmark as a dashed contour.
- `min_cell_n`: minimum cell size for the subsample mode. Cells with fewer
  observations return `NA`.

A typical pre-estimation workflow uses Somers' D, which is the most
theoretically aligned with QQR, followed by co-exceedance probability to
check for tail dependence:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## Pre-estimation: fit a minimal model (fastest; SEs not needed here)
fit_pre <- qqr(Y ~ X + W1, data = dat, qvar = "X",
               taus = taus, m = m, h = "silverman", se_type = "none")

## Somers' D -- recommended diagnostic
res_somers <- qqr_cor_heatmap(
  fit_pre,
  method      = "somers_d",
  mode        = "subsample",
  palette     = "RdBu",
  center_zero = TRUE,
  annotate    = TRUE,
  title       = "Pre-estimation: D(Y|X) -- does QQR add information?"
)

## Print console summary
print(res_somers)

## Display heatmap
res_somers$plot

## Save
ggplot2::ggsave("pre_somers.png", res_somers$plot,
                width = 9, height = 8, dpi = 300)

## Inspect the raw dependence matrix
round(res_somers$matrix, 3)
```

If the Somers' D matrix is approximately constant across cells — say, all
values within a narrow band around a common value — this suggests that the
dependence between \(X\) and \(Y\) is homogeneous and that QR would deliver
comparable results to QQR. If the matrix shows substantial variation,
particularly sign changes across the lower-left and upper-right corners of
the plot, this is non-parametric evidence for quantile-state-dependent
transmission that motivates QQR.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## Co-exceedance: tail dependence check
res_coex <- qqr_cor_heatmap(
  fit_pre,
  method            = "coexceedance",
  mode              = "subsample",
  palette           = "YlOrRd",
  center_zero       = FALSE,
  annotate          = TRUE,
  independence_line = TRUE,   ## dashed contour at (1-tau_i)(1-tau_j)
  title             = "Pre-estimation: Co-exceedance P(X >= Q_x, Y >= Q_y)"
)
res_coex$plot

## Blomqvist beta -- most robust for small cells
res_blomqvist <- qqr_cor_heatmap(
  fit_pre,
  method  = "blomqvist",
  mode    = "subsample",
  palette = "RdBu",
  title   = "Pre-estimation: Blomqvist beta (sign correlation)"
)
res_blomqvist$plot

## Binary mode (Roudane 2026 replication) -- for comparison only
res_binary <- qqr_cor_heatmap(
  fit_pre,
  method      = "spearman",
  mode        = "binary",
  palette     = "RdBu",
  center_zero = TRUE,
  annotate    = FALSE,
  title       = "Pre-estimation (Roudane 2026): binary Spearman"
)
res_binary$plot
```

These four calls in sequence — Somers' D, co-exceedance, Blomqvist beta and
Roudane binary Spearman — provide a comprehensive characterisation of the
pre-estimation dependence structure from multiple methodological angles. If all
four indicate substantial heterogeneity across the joint quantile grid, the
case for proceeding with QQR is strong and is supported by multiple
independent lines of evidence. If they agree that the dependence is
approximately uniform, the researcher has evidence-based grounds for
reporting QR rather than QQR and can document this decision explicitly.

The `qqr_cor_heatmap()` output can also be placed alongside the
post-estimation `qqr_heatmap()` output in a figure panel to show, for the
same dataset, how the raw bivariate dependence (pre-model) compares with
the estimated local slope surface (post-model). The shared `n_bins = length(taus)`
default ensures these two figures use the same grid and can be placed
side by side without re-scaling the axes.

# Example workflow

This section illustrates a basic workflow using simulated data. The example is deliberately simple and is designed to show how the R code maps to the mathematical objects defined earlier. It also demonstrates how the options for including or omitting the grid values propagate through the extract, export and comparison helpers.

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(qqrtools)

set.seed(1)
n  <- 300
X  <- rnorm(n)
W1 <- rnorm(n)
W2 <- rnorm(n)
U  <- rnorm(n)

## Simple data generating process with heterogeneous effect of X
## The effect of X on Y depends on an unobserved random quantile.
Y  <- 0.5 + X * qnorm(runif(n)) + 0.3 * W1 - 0.2 * W2 + U

dat <- data.frame(Y = Y, X = X, W1 = W1, W2 = W2)

## 1. Fit QQR model
taus <- seq(0.1, 0.9, by = 0.2)
m    <- 11

fit <- qqr(
  Y ~ X + W1 + W2,
  data    = dat,
  qvar    = "X",
  taus    = taus,
  m       = m,
  h       = "slope",       # automatic -- the default
  se_type = "ker"          # the default; use "boot" for final results
)

## Robust bandwidth alternative (preferred for heavy-tailed data)
## fit_robust <- qqr(Y ~ X + W1 + W2, data = dat, qvar = "X",
##                  taus = taus, m = m, h = "robust")

## Check-loss cross-validated bandwidth
## fit_cv <- qqr(Y ~ X + W1 + W2, data = dat, qvar = "X",
##               taus = taus, m = m, h = "cv_fast")

## Manual bandwidth (triggers reproducibility warning)
## fit_manual <- suppressWarnings(
##   qqr(Y ~ X + W1 + W2, data = dat, qvar = "X",
##       taus = taus, m = m, h = 0.4)
## )

## 2. Inspect the structure
fit
s <- summary(fit)
s

## 2b. Retrieve bandwidth details for the methods section
cat(s$h_details)
```

The object `fit` contains the full set of coefficient and p value surfaces described in Section 3.3, together with the grid, quantile vector and bandwidth diagnostics. The `h_details` field prints the selection formula, the numerical inputs, and the resulting bandwidth in a format ready to include in a paper's methods section.

```{r}
## 3. Extract the slope surface for X as a wide table
surf_X <- qqr_surface(
  fit,
  coef   = "X",
  what   = "coef",
  long   = FALSE,
  digits = 3
)

head(surf_X)
```

The object `surf_X` is a data frame representation of the slope surface \([\hat\beta_{ij}]\) for the quantile regressor, indexed by grid point and outcome quantile. Each row corresponds to a grid location \(z_i\), and each `tau_*` column corresponds to an outcome quantile \(\tau_j\).

```{r}
## 4. Compute row averages of the slope for all coefficients,
##    including the grid values is True by default
row_means <- rowave.qqr(fit, coef = "all", digits = 3,
                        include_grid_value = TRUE)
head(row_means)
```

The object `row_means` contains the row wise averages \(\bar\beta_{k,i}\) across quantiles for each coefficient \(k\), summarising how the average effect varies along the support of the quantile regressor. The first two columns record the grid index and underlying grid value used to centre the local regressions.

If a more compact representation is preferred, the grid values can be suppressed:

```{r}
## 4b. Row means without the grid values
row_means_compact <- rowave.qqr(fit, coef = "all", digits = 3,
                                include_grid_value = FALSE)
head(row_means_compact)
```

In this case only the integer grid index and the row means are retained. This is useful when the grid locations are documented elsewhere or when the table is to be merged with other summaries by index.

```{r}
## 5a. Static 3D plot of the slope surface for X
plot(fit, coef = "X", what = "coef", engine = "base")
```

This call plots the function \((z_i,\tau_j) \mapsto \hat\beta_{ij}\), providing a visual representation of how the marginal effect of `X` varies jointly across the distribution of \(X\) and the conditional quantiles of \(Y\).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## 5b. Smooth 3D surface using surface3d()
surface3d(fit, coef = "X",
          palette        = "viridis",
          add_zero_plane = TRUE,
          clim           = c(-2, 2),
          theta          = -30,
          phi            = 25)
```

`surface3d()` plots the full raw coefficient matrix as a smooth coloured surface, equivalent to MATLAB's `surf()`. The `add_zero_plane = TRUE` option superimposes a translucent reference plane at \(z = 0\) to help identify regions where the coefficient changes sign. Setting `clim` to a fixed range ensures that colours are directly comparable if multiple surfaces are plotted side by side.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## 5c. Ribbon panel plot using panel_surface()
panel_surface(fit,
              palette        = "RdBu",
              add_zero_plane = TRUE)
```

`panel_surface()` displays one coloured flat panel per coefficient, side by side, on a shared colour scale. This layout matches the style of several published QQR studies and provides a compact overview of all coefficient surfaces simultaneously.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## 5d. Interactive 3D surface using Int.plot()
Int.plot(fit, coef = "X", what = "coef",
         add_plane = TRUE, plane_z = 0)
```

---

This subsection provide a fully interactive
browser-based layer of visualisation built on the **plotly** engine.  Unlike the
static base-graphics functions above, these functions return `plotly` objects that
can be rotated, zoomed, hovered over, and saved either as self-contained HTML files
(for sharing) or as static PNG files (for publication).  All four functions share the
same **axis convention**: the x-axis shows the quantile regressor grid values
\(z_i\) and the y-axis shows the outcome quantile levels \(\tau_j\), so
that all four plots are mutually comparable when placed side-by-side.

---

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## 5e. Interactive heatmap of the coefficient surface using qqr_heatmap()

## Basic call: focal regressor, RdBu palette centred at zero.
## The x-axis shows the quantile regressor grid values z_i;
## the y-axis shows the outcome quantile levels tau.
## Each cell colour encodes the estimated coefficient beta_{ij}.
p_heat <- qqr_heatmap(fit)
p_heat
```

The default call to `qqr_heatmap()` produces a 2-D colour tile grid of the slope
surface \([\hat\beta_{ij}]\) for the focal quantile regressor.  Blue cells indicate
negative coefficients; red cells indicate positive ones; white marks cells near zero.
The diverging `"RdBu"` palette is centred at exactly zero by default
(`center_zero = TRUE`), so that sign changes are immediately visible regardless of
the overall scale of the surface.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## Overlay significance stars: cells with p < 0.01 are marked ***,
## p < 0.05 marked **, and p < 0.10 marked *.
## Requires the model to have been fitted with se_type != "none".
p_heat_stars <- qqr_heatmap(fit,
                             sig_overlay = "stars",
                             sig_levels  = c("***" = 0.01,
                                             "**"  = 0.05,
                                             "*"   = 0.10),
                             sig_size    = 12L,
                             sig_colour  = "black")
p_heat_stars
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## Dots overlay: any significant cell (p < 0.10) receives a filled bullet.
## Useful when the reader only needs to know which cells are significant
## rather than the exact significance level.
p_heat_dots <- qqr_heatmap(fit,
                            sig_overlay = "dots",
                            sig_colour  = "white",   # white text on dark cells
                            palette     = "Viridis")
p_heat_dots
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## P-value surface: shows where the estimated coefficient is statistically
## distinguishable from zero.  Use a sequential palette with no zero-centering.
p_heat_pval <- qqr_heatmap(fit,
                            what        = "pvalue",
                            palette     = "YlOrRd",
                            center_zero = FALSE)
p_heat_pval
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## All coefficients in a subplot grid.
## One panel per coefficient (intercept, X, W1, W2), all sharing the same
## colour scale.  This provides a compact overview of the full model surface.
p_heat_all <- qqr_heatmap(fit,
                           coef        = "all",
                           palette     = "RdBu",
                           sig_overlay = "stars")
p_heat_all
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## Fix colour limits to [-1.5, 1.5] for cross-model comparison.
## Useful when comparing fits on different sub-samples or with different
## bandwidths, so that colours have the same meaning across figures.
p_heat_fixed <- qqr_heatmap(fit, clim = c(-1.5, 1.5))
p_heat_fixed
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## Save as self-contained interactive HTML.
## The file can be opened in any web browser and distributed to co-authors.
htmlwidgets::saveWidget(p_heat_stars,
                        "qqr_heatmap_stars.html",
                        selfcontained = TRUE)

## Save as a static PNG for journal submission.
## Requires Python kaleido; install once with:
##   reticulate::py_install("kaleido")
qqr_heatmap(fit, sig_overlay = "stars",
            snapshot      = TRUE,
            snapshot_file = "qqr_heatmap_stars.png")
```

---

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## 5f. Interactive contour plot of the coefficient surface using qqr_contour()

## Basic call: filled contour with 10 levels, bold zero contour.
## The zero contour (drawn in black) marks the exact boundary where the
## estimated coefficient changes sign -- often the most economically
## meaningful feature of the QQR surface.
p_contour <- qqr_contour(fit)
p_contour
```

`qqr_contour()` complements the heatmap by connecting points of equal coefficient
value with iso-lines.  Contour plots make gradient directions and the precise
location of sign-change boundaries visible in a way that a simple colour grid
cannot.  The bold black zero contour is drawn automatically whenever zero falls
within the data range.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## Increase to 20 contour levels for finer resolution of the surface shape.
## Useful when the coefficient surface has rapid local variation.
p_contour_fine <- qqr_contour(fit, n_levels = 20L)
p_contour_fine
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## Significance mask: non-significant regions (p > 0.05) are greyed out
## with a semi-transparent overlay.  The colour underneath is still visible,
## but the grey overlay signals that those estimates should be interpreted
## with caution.  Requires se_type != "none" in the fitted model.
p_contour_mask <- qqr_contour(fit,
                               sig_mask      = TRUE,
                               sig_threshold = 0.05)
p_contour_mask
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## Suppress inline contour labels for a cleaner appearance.
## Useful for presentations or small figures where the labels become crowded.
p_contour_clean <- qqr_contour(fit, show_labels = FALSE)
p_contour_clean
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## P-value contour: shows where the effect is statistically significant.
## Use a sequential palette and suppress the zero contour (not meaningful
## for p-values, which are bounded at 0 and 1).
p_contour_pval <- qqr_contour(fit,
                               what         = "pvalue",
                               palette      = "YlOrRd",
                               center_zero  = FALSE,
                               zero_contour = FALSE,
                               n_levels     = 12L)
p_contour_pval
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## Fix colour limits and apply a significance mask simultaneously.
## This combination highlights exactly which parts of the surface are
## both large in magnitude and statistically significant.
p_contour_full <- qqr_contour(fit,
                               clim          = c(-2, 2),
                               sig_mask      = TRUE,
                               sig_threshold = 0.10,
                               n_levels      = 15L)
p_contour_full
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## Save the contour plot as an interactive HTML file.
htmlwidgets::saveWidget(p_contour_mask,
                        "qqr_contour_mask.html",
                        selfcontained = TRUE)

## Save as a static PNG for journal submission.
qqr_contour(fit,
            sig_mask      = TRUE,
            sig_threshold = 0.05,
            snapshot      = TRUE,
            snapshot_file = "qqr_contour_mask.png")
```

---

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## 5g. Unified interactive visualisation hub using qqr_plotly()

## qqr_plotly() is a single function that produces three different plot types
## depending on the `type` argument: "surface" (3-D), "heatmap" (2-D), or
## "contour" (2-D).  It is the most flexible of the four plotly functions
## and is a convenient entry point when the researcher has not yet decided
## which display type best communicates the result.

## 3-D interactive surface -- default Viridis palette.
## Click and drag to rotate; scroll to zoom; hover for exact values.
p_surf <- qqr_plotly(fit, type = "surface")
p_surf
```

The 3-D surface produced by `qqr_plotly(type = "surface")` maps each
grid--quantile pair \((z_i, \tau_j)\) to a point in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) with
height \(\hat\beta_{ij}\).  The interactive rendering allows the researcher to
inspect the surface from any angle, which is particularly valuable when the
surface has a complex saddle shape or multiple local extrema that are hard to
communicate in a single static view.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## 3-D surface with RdBu palette and a translucent red zero plane.
## The zero plane cuts the surface at beta = 0, making it immediately
## clear which (z_i, tau_j) combinations yield positive versus negative
## effects.  The opacity of the plane is controlled by zero_plane_opacity.
p_surf_rdbu <- qqr_plotly(fit,
                           type               = "surface",
                           colorscale         = "RdBu",
                           show_zero_plane    = TRUE,
                           zero_plane_opacity = 0.30,
                           center_zero        = TRUE)
p_surf_rdbu
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## 3-D surface with Jet palette and a custom camera angle.
## The camera argument sets the initial viewing position in x/y/z units.
## Adjusting aspect_ratio compresses the z-axis relative to x and y,
## which is useful when the coefficient surface is very flat.
p_surf_jet <- qqr_plotly(fit,
                          type         = "surface",
                          colorscale   = "Jet",
                          camera       = list(eye = list(x = 2.0,
                                                         y = 1.2,
                                                         z = 0.8)),
                          aspect_ratio = c(1, 1, 0.5))
p_surf_jet
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## 2-D heatmap via qqr_plotly() -- identical layout to qqr_heatmap().
## Use qqr_plotly(type = "heatmap") when you want the three display types
## accessible from a single function call for side-by-side comparison.
p_heat2 <- qqr_plotly(fit,
                       type        = "heatmap",
                       colorscale  = "RdBu",
                       sig_overlay = TRUE,
                       sig_symbol  = "*",
                       center_zero = TRUE)
p_heat2
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## 2-D contour via qqr_plotly() -- identical layout to qqr_contour().
p_contour2 <- qqr_plotly(fit,
                          type        = "contour",
                          colorscale  = "Viridis",
                          n_contours  = 15L,
                          show_labels = TRUE)
p_contour2
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## P-value surface as an interactive heatmap.
## Cells close to zero (dark) indicate highly significant estimates;
## cells near one (light) indicate non-significance.
p_pval_heat <- qqr_plotly(fit,
                           what       = "pvalue",
                           type       = "heatmap",
                           colorscale = "Plasma",
                           clim       = c(0, 1))
p_pval_heat
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## Save the 3-D surface as a self-contained interactive HTML file.
## This is the recommended format for sharing with co-authors or uploading
## as supplementary material, as it requires no R installation to view.
p_surf_final <- qqr_plotly(fit,
                            type            = "surface",
                            colorscale      = "RdBu",
                            show_zero_plane = TRUE,
                            center_zero     = TRUE)
htmlwidgets::saveWidget(p_surf_final,
                        "qqr_surface_interactive.html",
                        selfcontained = TRUE)

## Save the heatmap as a static PNG.
qqr_plotly(fit,
           type          = "heatmap",
           colorscale    = "RdBu",
           snapshot      = TRUE,
           snapshot_file = "qqr_heatmap_plotly.png")
```

---

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## 5h. Pre-model quantile dependence diagnostic using qqr_cor_heatmap()

## qqr_cor_heatmap() is a pre-model diagnostic that visualises the raw
## bivariate dependence structure between the quantile regressor X and the
## dependent variable Y before any QQR model is fitted.  It partitions
## the joint distribution of (X, Y) into an n_bins x n_bins grid of
## quantile cells and computes a chosen dependence measure within each cell.
##
## AXIS CONVENTION: the x-axis shows the X (regressor) quantile probability
## levels and the y-axis shows the Y (dependent variable) quantile probability
## levels.  Both axes use the exact tau levels from the fitted model
## (e.g. 0.05, 0.10, ..., 0.95 when taus = seq(0.05, 0.95, by = 0.05)),
## so each cell of the heatmap aligns directly with one cell of the QQR
## coefficient surface.
##
## Six dependence measures are available:
##   "spearman"     -- Spearman rank correlation (default; robust, range [-1,1])
##   "kendall"      -- Kendall's tau-b (robust for small cells; range [-1,1])
##   "somers_d"     -- Somers' D(Y|X) (directional; mirrors QQR structure)
##   "pearson"      -- Pearson linear correlation (range [-1,1])
##   "blomqvist"    -- Blomqvist's beta (most robust; range [-1,1])
##   "coexceedance" -- Joint tail exceedance probability (range [0,1])
##
## Two computation modes are available:
##   "subsample" (default) -- computes the measure on observations within
##                            each joint quantile cell
##   "binary"              -- replicates Roudane (2026): correlates binary
##                            indicators I(X <= Q_X(tau)) and I(Y <= Q_Y(tau))
##                            across the full sample

## Default: Spearman rank correlation in subsample mode.
## The result is a list with $plot (plotly), $matrix (numeric matrix),
## $x_breaks, $y_breaks, $cell_n, $method, and $mode.
result_spearman <- qqr_cor_heatmap(fit)
result_spearman$plot    ## display the interactive heatmap
result_spearman$matrix  ## access the raw dependence matrix for further analysis
```

The return value of `qqr_cor_heatmap()` is a named list of class
`"qqr_cor_heatmap"`.  The `$plot` element is the `plotly` object and
renders directly in the RStudio Viewer.  The `$matrix` element is the raw
\(n\_bins \times n\_bins\) numeric matrix of dependence values, which can be
used for further analysis or exported independently.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## Print a concise console summary: method, mode, grid dimensions, value
## range, mean, number of NA cells, and quick-save instructions.
print(result_spearman)
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## Somers' D(Y|X): the directional rank association measure that most
## closely mirrors the causal structure of QQR (Y is the outcome, X is
## the regressor).  D(Y|X) != D(X|Y), so it is asymmetric in a way that
## Spearman and Kendall are not.
result_somers <- qqr_cor_heatmap(fit, method = "somers_d")
result_somers$plot
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## Blomqvist's beta: uses only the signs of deviations from cell medians.
## The most robust choice when the data are sparse in some cells, for
## example when n is small relative to n_bins^2.
result_blomqvist <- qqr_cor_heatmap(fit, method = "blomqvist")
result_blomqvist$plot
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## Kendall's tau-b: a robust alternative to Spearman that handles ties
## more gracefully and is preferred when cell sizes are small.
result_kendall <- qqr_cor_heatmap(fit, method = "kendall")
result_kendall$plot
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## Co-exceedance probability with the independence benchmark contour.
## Each cell shows P(X >= Q_X(tau_i), Y >= Q_Y(tau_j)), i.e. the
## probability that both variables simultaneously exceed their respective
## tau-level quantiles.  The dashed contour marks the independence
## benchmark (1-tau_i)(1-tau_j): cells above this contour exhibit positive
## tail dependence; cells below exhibit negative tail dependence.
result_coex <- qqr_cor_heatmap(fit,
                                method            = "coexceedance",
                                independence_line = TRUE)
result_coex$plot
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## Binary indicator mode: replicates Roudane (2026).
## Correlates I(X <= Q_X(tau_i)) with I(Y <= Q_Y(tau_j)) across the full
## sample using Spearman rank correlation.  This mode is provided for
## reproducibility with the original paper; the subsample mode is
## methodologically preferable for most applications.
result_binary <- qqr_cor_heatmap(fit,
                                  method = "spearman",
                                  mode   = "binary")
result_binary$plot
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## Custom grid size: use a coarser 9 x 9 grid.
## Useful when the sample size is small relative to the default n_bins,
## because smaller cells contain fewer observations and may produce NA
## values when the chosen measure cannot be computed (min_cell_n = 3).
result_coarse <- qqr_cor_heatmap(fit, n_bins = 9L)
result_coarse$plot
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## Suppress cell annotations for a cleaner figure on fine grids.
## The annotate = FALSE option removes the numeric values printed inside
## each cell; useful for large grids (e.g. 19 x 19) where the annotations
## become crowded.
result_noann <- qqr_cor_heatmap(fit, annotate = FALSE)
result_noann$plot
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## Fix colour limits to [-1, 1] to match the full theoretical range of
## the Spearman measure.  Useful for cross-variable comparisons, e.g.
## when computing the diagnostic for X vs Y and for W1 vs Y side-by-side.
result_fixed <- qqr_cor_heatmap(fit, clim = c(-1, 1))
result_fixed$plot
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## Inspect and export the raw dependence matrix.
## The $matrix element has rows indexed by X quantile bins and columns
## indexed by Y quantile bins, consistent with the axis convention.
print(result_spearman)       ## console summary
heatmap(result_spearman$matrix,
        main  = "Spearman quantile dependence (base R heatmap)")

## Save as a self-contained interactive HTML file.
htmlwidgets::saveWidget(result_somers$plot,
                        "qqr_cor_heatmap_somers.html",
                        selfcontained = TRUE)

## Save as a static PNG for journal submission (requires kaleido).
## Install once with: reticulate::py_install("kaleido")
qqr_cor_heatmap(fit,
                method        = "somers_d",
                snapshot      = TRUE,
                snapshot_file = "qqr_cor_heatmap_somers.png")
```

The `qqr_cor_heatmap()` diagnostic is most informative when read alongside the
fitted QQR coefficient surface.  If the dependence heatmap is approximately
uniform -- showing similar values across all quantile cells -- then the marginal
effect of \(X\) on \(Y\) does not vary much across the joint distribution, and a
standard quantile regression may suffice.  Substantial heterogeneity in the
dependence measure, particularly asymmetry between the lower-left and upper-right
corners of the grid, motivates the full QQR analysis and helps interpret the
resulting coefficient surface.

---

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## 6. Export all surfaces to Excel, including grid values
excel.qqr(fit,
          file               = "QQR_example.xlsx",
          which              = "both",
          include_grid_value = TRUE,
          digits             = 3)
```

The Excel file produced by `excel.qqr()` contains a worksheet for each coefficient, with separate sheets for coefficient values and p values. The leading columns indicate the grid index and grid value. These tables preserve the link between coefficients, grid points and quantiles and can be imported into other software or included directly in reports.

A more compact export that omits the grid values can also be requested:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
excel.qqr(fit,
          file               = "QQR_example_compact.xlsx",
          which              = "both",
          include_grid_value = FALSE,
          digits             = 3)
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## 7a. Export coefficients and p-values for X to Word (separate tables)
word.qqr(
  fit,
  file               = "QQR_X_surfaces.docx",
  coef               = "X",
  which              = "both",
  digits             = 3,
  include_grid_value = TRUE
)

## 7b. Export coefficients with significance stars (combined table)
word.qqr(
  fit,
  file               = "QQR_X_stars.docx",
  coef               = "X",
  which              = "coef_stars",
  digits             = 3,
  include_grid_value = TRUE
)
```

The `"coef_stars"` option produces a single publication-ready table with significance stars appended directly to each coefficient. P values that could not be computed are marked `[NA]` rather than left blank, and an automatic footnote is appended explaining the star conventions. This is the format most commonly used in empirical papers that report QQR results.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## 8. Compare QR and row--mean QQR for X
cmp_X <- compare.qqr(fit, coef = "X", digits = 3)
head(cmp_X)
```

The object `cmp_X` has one row per quantile level `tau` and two coefficient columns,`qr` and `qqr_mean`. These correspond respectively to the standard QR estimate \(\hat\beta^{\mathrm{QR}}(\tau_k)\) and to the grid-averaged QQR estimate \(\hat{\bar\beta}(\tau_k)\) derived from the slope surface for `X`.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## 9. Export QR--QQR comparisons to Excel and Word
excel.compare.qqr(fit,
                  file = "QQR_QR_comparison_X.xlsx",
                  coef = "X",
                  digits = 3)

word.compare.qqr(fit,
                 file  = "QQR_QR_comparison_X.docx",
                 coef  = "X",
                 digits = 3)
```

These helpers create compact comparison tables for inclusion in appendices or supplementary material that document how closely the averaged QQR effects track the standard QR coefficients across quantiles.

```{r, message = FALSE}
## 10. Plot QR and row--mean QQR coefficients for X
# library(ggplot2)

# p_X <- plot.compare.qqr(fit, coef = "X",
#                        xlab = "Quantile level (tau)",
#                        ylab = "Coefficient",
#                        legend_title = "Model")

# p_X
```

The resulting `ggplot` object displays two curves as functions of \(\tau\), one for the QR coefficients and one for the row--mean QQR coefficients. In simulated designs where the QQR model is correctly specified, the two curves should be close. In empirical applications, systematic deviations can signal that the richer QQR surface is detecting patterns that the global QR model overlooks.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
## 11. Inspect and customise the plot further if needed
p_X + theme_minimal()
```

This completes a typical workflow from fitting a QQR model, through surface extraction and averaging, to QR--QQR comparison, export and visualisation using the tools provided in `qqrtools`.
